content.content: 70 minutes, 35 Questions
In its Dry State, the mixture of atmospheric gases contains two main constituents, nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%) by volume.
The remaining 1% is made up of a multitude of different gases.
This composition has no measurable variations up to a height of some 80 km.
There is always some water vapour (water in a gas state) present in the atmosphere, the amount depending greatly on the temperature and the history of the air.
The warmer the air, the greater its ability to hold water as a gas.
Generally, water vapour in measurable quantities is found below 6-7 km (20000 feet).
Its main source is evaporation of water from oceans, waterways, lakes etc. Plant transpiration is also a substantial provider of water vapour.
Water has a dramatic effect on the weather, this is because water vapour changes to water or ice.
This can yield cloud, rain, fog, hail and other phenomena.
It therefore can be seen that water vapour is added to the atmosphere by evaporation while it returns to Earth through condensation and subsequent descent.
This is a compound gas. It is a colourless, heavy gas with scarcely any smell.
Carbon dioxide is produced by the oxidation process e.g., when petrol is burned in an engine.

When items such as paper or plastics are burnt in a fire, their carbon content is converted to CO2. The important thing about carbon dioxide is that when it is present in the atmosphere, it absorbs terrestrial (Earth) radiation, which in turn, influences the temperature of the air surrounding the Earth.
This is the cause of the Greenhouse Effect.
Ozone molecules are formed in the upper levels of the stratosphere and the lower levels of the Mesosphere.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun and as a result, sinks to the lower levels of the Stratosphere.
It is generally accepted that some 60% of harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun is absorbed by this ozone layer.
In addition to the gases mentioned so far, the atmosphere contains particles such as salt from evaporating sea water, dust and other particles.
These particles influence visibility and on incoming solar radiation and therefore have a large effect on the atmospheric temperature.
The condensation process relies on these solid particles.
If there is an overabundance of solid particles, such as in polluted air, the condensation process can occur prematurely.

lessons.title: The Vertical Division Within the Atmosphere

content.content: There are several reasonably well-defined layers within the atmosphere, temperature being the distinguishing feature.
The lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which almost all the water vapour and approximately 75% of all molecular mass is found.
This is the layer in which weather and turbulence phenomena are most marked.
The layer is capped by the Tropopause. It varies in mean height between some 18 km over the Equator to 8 km over the Poles.
Jetstreams are often associated with the breaks in the Tropopause.
The temperature lapse rate (reduction of temperature with height) within the Tropopause is fairly constant and averages about 2°C/1000ft.
The temperature lapse rate can reverse itself i.e., a rise in temperature with height, this is known as an inversion and the layer of air within which it occurs is said to have a negative lapse rate.
Temperature can also remain constant with height; this is known as isothermal.
The lower part of the Stratosphere is isothermal.
The temperature at the Tropopause varies quite dramatically in certain situations.
The overriding influence on the height of the Tropopause, and therefore its temperature, is the temperature lapse rate, air density and the surface temperature.
Over the Equator where low level temperatures are naturally high, density of air is less.
This means that the column of less dense air is quite stretched out, so that the top is very high.
With a constant temperature lapse rate of 2°C/1000ft, the temperature at the Tropopause will be extremely low.
The Tropopause is highest and the coldest over the Equator.
The Tropopause is lowest and the warmest over the Poles.
The Tropopause height varies in mid latitudes and is warmer than over the Equator but colder than over the Poles.
As mentioned, the main reason for the differences in height of the Tropopause lies in the fact that density of air is less over the Equator and greater over the Poles.
In turn, the main reason for this dissimilarity is the difference in surface temperature due to varying angles of insolation, solar input.
This layer in the atmosphere above the Tropopause has a thickness of some 35 km.
Initially, above the Tropopause the layer is isothermal for some 8-10 km.
Above this height, the temperature slowly increases and towards the top quarter temperatures increase rather strongly with height.
The reason for this rapid increase in temperature is the large amount of ultraviolet radiation absorbed by the ozone layer.
Because of the isothermal layer of the lower Stratosphere, any cloud or weather generally will not penetrate into the Stratosphere.
An aerosol is a mixture of fine, solid particles or liquid droplets, in air or another gas.

Aerosols can be natural or anthropogenic. Examples of natural aerosols are fog, dust, sea salt, volcanic ash, forest exudates (a fluid emitted by an organism through pores or a wound) and geyser steam.
Examples of anthropogenic aerosols are haze, particulate air pollutants and smoke.
Effectively, they are any tiny solid particle with a crystalline structure at the molecular level.
Water vapour and aerosols are the building blocks for all cloud and hence precipitation as well.
Inside every single cloud droplet, there is an aerosol.
Just like water vapour, all aerosols originate from the surface of the earth, so the higher we go, the less of these elements we encounter.
Above the Tropopause, there is virtually no water vapour and almost no aerosols; hence there is little or no cloud in the Stratosphere or above.
Several types of atmospheric aerosol have a significant effect on Earth's climate:
Volcanic,
Desert dust,
Sea-salt,
that originating from Biogenic sources
- Human-made.
Volcanic aerosol forms in the Stratosphere after an eruption as droplets of sulfuric acid that can prevail for up to two years, and reflect sunlight, lowering temperature.
Mineral particles blown to high altitudes, absorb heat and may be responsible for inhibiting storm cloud formation.
Primarily from burning oil and coal, affect the behaviour of clouds.
Volcanic eruptions release large amounts of sulphuric acid, hydrogen sulphide and hydrochloric acid into the atmosphere.
These gases represent aerosols and eventually return to Earth as acid rain, having several adverse effects on the environment and human life.
Aerosols interact with the Earth's energy budget in two ways, directly and indirectly.

A direct effect, is that aerosols scatter sunlight directly back into space. This can lead to a significant decrease in the temperature, being an additional element to the Greenhouse Effect and therefore contributing to the global climate change.

The indirect effects refer to the aerosols interfering with formations that interact directly with radiation. For example, they can modify the size of the cloud particles in the lower atmosphere, thereby changing the way clouds reflect and absorb light and therefore modifying the Earth's energy budget.

When aerosols absorb pollutants, it facilitates the deposition of pollutants to the surface of the Earth, as well as to bodies of water. This has the potential to be damaging to both the environment and human health.
Temperature is a measure of heat contained within a body.
It can also be seen in terms of a body’s ability to give off heat to another body or to receive it from another body.
The three main units of measurement of temperature are:
Celsius
Fahrenheit
Kelvin
0° Celsius is the temperature of melting of pure ice under standard conditions.
100° Celsius is the boiling point of pure water under the same conditions.
The Fahrenheit scale is not generally used in NZ.
The Kelvin scale uses the same size unit as Celsius but has no negative units.
Surface air temperature is measured at approx. 1 ½ metres above the ground.
The thermometer is placed in a Stevenson Screen, a louvred box arrangement, which ensures that sunlight does not fall on the thermometer.

lessons.title: How Does Air Temperature Effect Landing?

content.content: A sealed runway on a hot day will be giving off a lot more thermal energy than a grass runway.
This causes us to have more thermal turbulence on the approach and a longer float during the flare, causing us to use more runway before touching down.
E.g., The Diamond on a hot day.
Radiation is the movement, passage, or transmission of heat from one body to another without the use of intermediary matter such as air.
The transmission of radiation energy is in the form of electromagnetic waves.
If a body emits radiation, its temperature will drop.
If a body receives radiation, its temperature will increase.
The temperature of the body emitting the radiation determines the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation.
The hotter the body, the shorter the wavelength and vice versa.
The two types of radiation we need to understand are:
Solar Radiation
Terrestrial Radiation
Virtually all the atmospheric energy is derived from the Sun.
Because of the very high source temperatures involved, solar radiation is short wave radiation.
Solar radiation is made up of approx.:
Ultraviolet 9%
Visible light 45%
Infrared 46%
A large amount of the ultraviolet radiation is absorbed by the ozone layer.
A large part of the visible light is absorbed by water vapour.

Some of the radiation received by the Earth is reflected back into space by cloud tops, while particles within the atmosphere prevent some solar radiation reaching the Earth’s surface due to scattering.
The scattered solar radiation that does reach the Earth’s surface is known as sky radiation.
Thus, the total solar radiation received by the Earth is the sum of sky radiation and direct radiation and is called global solar radiation.
There are three main factors that affect the amount of solar radiation the Earth receives:
Distance between the Sun and Earth.
Altitude of the Sun.
Length of the day.
The distance between the Sun and Earth varies during the year, producing the seasonal variations in solar energy received.
Because the Earth’s spin axis is not at right angles to the incoming solar radiation, the amount of insolation varies.
When the angle of Sun’s rays to the Earth is 90° or nearly so, the solar energy per square metre is more than when the angle is oblique.
The Poles, during their Winter, have nil insolation.
Because of the Earth’s spin axis, the length of day varies with latitude and season.
Hours of dark and light are equal over the world twice a year, on or about the 22nd March and 22nd September. These dates are known as the Equinoxes.
A solstice is an event that occurs when the sun appears to reach its most Northerly or Southerly excursion relative to the celestial Equator on the celestial sphere.
Two solstices occur annually.
Around 21st June and 21st December.
Instruments which measure solar radiation are called pyranometers.

These instruments use a sensing element consisting of alternating black and white wedge-shaped thin copper sectors. The white sectors are highly reflective, whereas the black sectors are highly absorbent.
The temperature difference between these sectors is a measure of radiation intensity.
The Earth’s temperature is far less than that of the Sun’s, the radiation emitted by it is long wave.
This radiation is called terrestrial radiation and consists of only infrared radiation.
The terrestrial radiation emitted is generally replenished by incoming solar radiation and thus an approximate balance exists between incoming and outgoing radiation.
Water vapour, cloud droplets, carbon dioxide and ozone are strong absorbers of terrestrial radiation and in turn emit energy themselves and heat the atmosphere to some extent.
Terrestrial radiation is therefore the energy transmitted by the Earth and the atmosphere.
There are a band of wavelengths where terrestrial radiation escapes readily from the atmosphere, this is referred to as the atmospheric window.
An approximate balance is reached annually between the amount of solar radiation received and terrestrial radiation emitted.
This balance is referred to as the energy budget and means that the average global temperature due to radiation is around 15°C.

lessons.title: Effect of Solar and Terrestrial Radiation on Air Temperature

content.content: The Earth’s atmosphere is warmed from below.
Incoming solar radiation excites the surface molecules which causes the surface to heat up.
This creates a hotplate effect which warms the air above the surface.
This hotplate effect will continue so long as the incoming solar radiation is more than the outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The warmed surface transfers the heat to the atmosphere through two main processes:
Conduction.
Convection.
Conduction is the transfer of heat through intermolecular action (touching).
The excited Earth molecules mix with the air molecules that are in touch with the surface and transfer sensible heat.
Air is a poor conductor of heat, so for heating of the atmosphere to take place, convection is required.

Once conduction has warmed a thin layer above the surface, convection occurs, where warmed air particles rise and are mixed with cooler ones at higher levels to give a general warming of the atmosphere.
Advection heat transfer differs from convection in that the movement of heat is confined to the horizontal plane.

This type of heat transfer is not powered by variations in density, but rather requires an outside force, such as wind or currents, to displace the particles of the medium. As the particles move horizontally into systems that are hotter or colder, heat is transferred.
Latent heat also warms the atmosphere.
Latent heat relates to the amount of energy required or given off by a substance to change state.
This latent heat does not affect the temperature of the substance undergoing the change.
The latent heat given off by water vapour changing to liquid water will warm the atmosphere.
At night, convection will eventually cease, and a general cooling of the atmosphere will take place.
It has been established that over a 24-hour period, a cycle of air temperature changes takes place due to changing temperatures of the Earth’s surface.
A graph can be drawn to represent the diurnal variation of surface temperature.
The maximum temperature will occur around 2pm, and the minimum around dawn.
The oscillation of the graph is affected by several factors which are often based on the surface's albedo.
Albedo is the ability of a surface to reject or reflect incoming solar radiation.
Any surface which heats quickly and cools just as quickly (deserts), will involve a wildly undulating diurnal variation of temperature.
Any surface that resists insolation or holds the insolation will have a mildly or nil fluctuating curve.
Maritime climates rarely have extremes of temperature.
The reasons for this are:
Specific Heat
By this is meant, the amount of thermal heat units required to raise the temperature of a unit mass by 1°C.
Water requires a large amount of specific heat.
Thus, when solar energy enters the water of oceans, vast amounts of energy are required to change the temperature by just a few degrees.
Over a given period of time per season, the amount of insolation is fairly static, and therefore so too is the surface temperature.
Thus, the diurnal variation of surface temperature curve will be almost straight.
Mixing
The solar energy received is mixed through a large layer by swells and currents etc., this will slow down the change in water temperature.
Again, the diurnal variation of surface temperature curve will be fairly straight.
Evaporation
Solar input will try to evaporate some water, demanding latent heat.
If the surface temperature had risen it would soon fall again as a result of the demand for latent heat.
Again, the diurnal variation of surface temperature curve will be fairly straight.
The Wind
Winds are generally stronger over the oceans than the land, due to reduced surface friction.
Any wind will cause mixing of the air and cause the air temperature to even out at a lower figure over a horizontal distance.
This will again straighten out the curve.
Water vapour is a good absorber of terrestrial radiation and in turn becomes a radiator of heat.
Therefore, an abundance of water vapour will cause an evening out of the surface temperature day or night and so too the graph.
Any cloud cover will have a two-fold effect.
Some of the solar radiation will be reflected into space, reducing the amount of solar radiation reaching the surface.
Terrestrial radiation will be absorbed by the cloud and will heat the atmosphere.
The overall result will be an evening out of the curve.
The wind will again cause mixing and an evening out of the temperature.
Therefore, the diurnal temperature variation graph will be shallower in windy conditions and more oscillating in calm conditions.
There is a great difference in the amount of heat energy received and emitted around the globe.
The result of these differences is the considerable lateral transfer of heat which takes place annually and these transfers have a strong effect on the world’s weather patterns.
This will be covered in greater detail later.
Climates can be classified in terms of annual range of temperature as follows:
Oceanic:
The annual range varies less than 10°C.
Maritime:
The annual range varies between 10 and 20°C.
Continental:
The annual range is greater than 20°C.
Atmospheric pressure is a force per unit area acting on each square metre of surface.
The unit of pressure is the Pascal.
Near the Earth’s surface, the atmosphere exerts a pressure of about 100,000 Pascals.
Because of the size of the unit hectopascals (hPa) are used.
The instrument used to measure pressure is the barometer.
It is essential that you know how high you are above the ground, especially when flying in mountainous terrain.
This is done using the altimeter, instrument that indicates the height of the aircraft above a set reference point.
But altimeters don’t measure height – instead, they measure pressure.
The altimeter in your aircraft is essentially a barometer which measures air pressure, not height, in its internal workings.
Through a series of linkages, this pressure reading is converted to a height which is displayed on the front dial of the instrument.

A second instrument on your instrument panel – the ‘vertical speed indicator’ or VSI also works by measuring changes in pressure as your aircraft climbs or descends and converts these changes to vertical speeds.
Basically, atmospheric pressure is the result of the weight of air.
If we consider a column of air, there is going to be more pressure at sea level than at 5000ft, where there is less air above in our column.
The reduction of air pressure with height is called a lapse rate, this lapse rate is dependent on the density of the air which is determined by the temperature.
If we consider two columns of air, one warm and one cold, the lapse rate will be greater in the cold (high density) column of air.
The number of feet lost per hectopascal lost is known as the pressure lapse rate, and it equates to:
30ft per one hectopascal lost.
Atmospheric pressure plays a large part in the production of ‘weather’.
It is therefore important to have a large-scale measure of pressure, more importantly sea level pressure and a way of presenting it on paper.
There are many stations which measure atmospheric pressure at their individual locations, corrections are applied to provide a sea level pressure, and these are collated to give the big picture.
These sea level pressures are drawn on our charts as isobars.
An isobar is a line joining places of equal pressures.
Depending on the map scale required, these isobars can be drawn at 2 hPa, 4 hPa or any other spacing.
There are a few basic rules that apply to isobars and their use:
They may be straight or curved.
They never cross or touch except when two ends of an isobar join to make a closed curving pattern.
Everywhere along an isobar, higher pressures are always on the same side and the same applies for lower pressures remaining on their side.
Ignoring the finer points, the wind flows parallel to the isobars.
The closeness of the isobars is a function of the pressure gradient which, in turn, determines the speed of the air flow.
Pressure patterns plotted on a weather map fall into two categories:
ANTICYCLONES (HIGHS)
DEPRESSIONS (LOWS, CYCLONES)
Pressures are highest at the centre.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the wind flows in an anti-clockwise direction around the centre.
One of the major characteristics of anticyclones is ‘surface divergence’, meaning at the surface, air moves out and away from the high.
This means that air within the high is ‘subsiding’, and high level ‘convergence’ is taking place.
Pressures are lowest at the centre.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the wind flows in a clockwise direction around the centre.
Lows are associated with surface convergence and air is rising within, creating high level divergence.
It can be seen that Highs and Lows form closed circuits, and on a global scale this is often the case.
This is simply an extension off an anticyclone.
Pressures are always lower of either side of the axis of the ridge.
An extension off a low.
Pressures are higher either side of the axis of the trough.
This is an area between two highs and two lows.
Winds are most likely to be light and variable.
In general, pressure systems tend to move from West to East.
This means that at any one position, the pressure is continually changing.
One change in atmospheric pressure is caused by temperature influences, this is known as the semi-diurnal variation of pressure.
A diurnal cycle means a ‘daily’ or ’24-hour’ cycle.
At approximately 1600 hours, the pressure drop is maximum.
Pressures increase beyond this time, and peak around 2200 hours.
A further decrease begins, dropping to the lowest value at around 0400.
From this point, the pressure again rises to a peak at around 1000 hours.
Note the variation takes place twice in 24 hours, hence the name semi-diurnal.
ISA is the ‘average’ condition of the atmosphere.
This average considers the very warm temperatures found near the Equator and the extremely cold conditions found at the Poles.
New Zealand sits in the mid-latitudes, experiences conditions both these extremes.
Our average conditions are close to those quoted in ISA, but there are variations between the far North and the far South of the country, and between Summer and Winter.
Atmospheric pressure shows a diurnal or semi-diurnal (twice-daily) cycle caused by global atmospheric tides.
This effect is strongest in tropical zones, with an amplitude of a few Hectopascals, and almost zero in polar areas.
In nature, air will always flow from high to low pressure.
The rate at which it flows mainly depends on the value of the pressure systems and their distance apart.
Pressure gradient is the change of pressure with horizontal distance measured from high to low.
The pressure gradient (a force) can be steep or shallow and its strength determines the speed the air flows from high to low.
The pressure gradient always acts at right angles to the isobars.
However, for reasons to be explained, the wind usually flows parallel to the isobars.
Engine performance, airframe performance and instrument operations all depend on atmospheric pressure and temperature.

If a prediction of how an engine or aircraft is going to perform is required, we need to know how it would perform with respect to a set of benchmark conditions and compare those conditions with the prevailing conditions.
The set of benchmark conditions are given by the International Standard Atmosphere (ISA).
ISA assumes the following conditions:
Air is dry and of a constant composition at all altitudes.
The pressure at sea level is 1013.25 hectopascals.
The air temperature at sea level is +15°C.
The temperature lapse rate is 1.98°C per 1000 feet up to an altitude of 36,090 feet above which the temperature is considered to be isothermal at –56.5°C.
The force of gravity is constant at 9.8 m/sec2.
The air’s density is 1.225 kg/m³.
These values are, in reality, fairly accurate in terms of global averages within the atmosphere but they may well be totally different in local situations.
Altimeters give us the height above a given pressure datum – in most cases mean sea level pressure.
As the sea level pressure changes, we must be able to adjust the pressure datum to maintain accurate altimeter readings.
The subscale provides the means to adjust the datum.
QNH
This is the Atmospheric pressure obtained from stations and reduced to mean sea level using ISA values.
With QNH set, the altimeter reads absolute altitude more commonly referred to as just altitude.
QFE
This is the ambient atmospheric pressure at a given datum.
With QFE set, the altimeter reads height above the datum.
QNE
This is the altimeter setting of 1013.2 hPa.
With QNE set, the altimeter will read pressure altitude, which is the altitude in ISA where the prevailing atmospheric pressure occurs.
QFF
This is the atmospheric pressure from stations, reduced to mean sea level using existing atmospheric values.
Not normally used.
Since the air pressure may change from day to day or even hour-to-hour, the altimeter must be calibrated to operate accurately at whatever the current air pressure is.
To facilitate changes in MSL pressure, the altimeter has a subscale adjustment.
It is essential that the correct QNH pressure (or QFE if applicable) is set on the altimeter sub-scale.
All altimeters are calibrated to ISA conditions.
The atmosphere rarely, if ever, conforms to ISA, therefore the height indicated by your altimeter is not necessarily the true height of your aircraft above the pressure surface set on the altimeter.
The errors become quite large at high altitudes; however, all altimeters will be experiencing the same errors – so vertical separations are maintained.
There are four forces which influence the strength and direction of the wind:
Pressure Gradient
Coriolis Force (also known as Geostrophic Force)
Centripetal Force
Friction Forces
Pressure gradient is the change in pressure with horizontal distance measured from high to low.
The pressure gradient force acts at right angles to the isobars, from high to low.
The closer together the isobars, the greater the pressure gradient.
In general, for a given isobar spacing, the wind becomes stronger with height.
Coriolis force originates in the Earth's rotation.
Any object which breaks contact with the Earth will follow a curved path in relation to the Earth’s surface.
The Earth rotates at the Equator at approx. 1000 mph.
However, the Poles rotate at near zero.
If an object departs from the Equator, the rotational speed of the Equator is imparted to it.
As the object travels towards the Poles (slower rotation), it would appear from the surface that the object travels on a curved path.
From space, the path would appear straight.
In the Southern Hemisphere, departing air from a high will curve to the left.
Coriolis force always acts at right angles to the flow of air.
Air that should flow from high to low pressure at right angles to the isobars is curved by Coriolis force.
Coriolis force is formulated as:
Another important thing to consider, is that Coriolis force always acts at right angles to the flow of air.

lessons.title: Pressure Gradient and Coriolis Force Interaction

content.content: The combined effect of the pressure gradient and Coriolis force is to cause the wind to blow parallel to the isobars.
Flow starts from a high ,under the influence of the pressure gradient, but is immediately influenced by Coriolis force acting at right angles, which turns it to the right.
Eventually the two forces become in line with each other but in opposite directions, and the flow runs parallel to the isobars.
It can be seen that in the Southern Hemisphere, the wind flow is anti-clockwise around a high and the Coriolis force acts towards the centre of the high.
Wind flow around a low is clockwise and the pressure gradient acts towards the centre.
All this is the theoretical situation; however, nothing is black and white in nature.

lessons.title: Centripetal Force – Geostrophic and Gradient Wind

content.content: When the wind follows straight isobars, pressure gradient and Coriolis force equal and opposite, it is a geostrophic wind.
When the wind follows curved isobars, it is a gradient wind.
As we know, isobars are not always straight, there must be a centre seeking (centripetal) force.
This centripetal force is known as the Cyclostrophic Force.
When pressure gradient and Coriolis force are equal, isobars will be straight, and the wind is geostrophic.
When pressure gradient and Coriolis force are not equal, isobars will be curved and the wind is gradient, the dominating force provides the centripetal force.
Because Coriolis force is little or nil at the Equator, pressures are relatively static in Equatorial regions.
Properties of the Coriolis force:
Acts on objects not rigidly attached to the Earth.
Always acts to deflect an object to the right (left) of its direction of motion in the Northern (Southern) Hemisphere.
Magnitude is zero at the Equator, maximum at the Poles.
Magnitude depends on the rotation rate of the Earth - the magnitude would increase if the Earth’s rotation rate increased.
If the Earth were not rotating, the Coriolis force would be zero.
The wind flow over the Earth experiences drag and slows down, the rougher the surface, the greater the drag and the slower the wind.
The layer in which this takes place is known as the Friction Layer and is generally assumed to be 2000ft deep.
The depth of the friction layer is dependent on roughness of the surface–rougher = deeper.
Remember that Coriolis force is proportional to the speed of the airflow.
If the wind slows down due to frictional forces, Coriolis force will decrease, and the pressure gradient will dominate.
A deep friction layer will mean the surface wind:
Is weaker than the wind above the friction layer.
Flows at a relatively large angle across the isobars towards the low.
A shallow friction layer, such as over oceans, will mean the surface wind:
Is almost as strong as the wind above the friction layer.
Flows at a fairly small angle across the surface isobars to the centre of the low.
As a rule:
Over the land, the speed of the wind will decrease by 2/3, and the angle across the isobars will be 30°.
Over the oceans, the speed of the wind will decrease by about 1/3, and the angle across the isobars will be about 10°.

A wind gust is a sudden, brief increase in the speed of the wind followed by a lull. According to National Weather Service observing practice, gusts are reported when the peak wind speed reaches at least 16kts and the variation in wind speed between the peaks and lulls is at least about 9Kts. Lasts about 20s.
For a gust to be reported in a METAR, METAR AUTO etc, the gust speed must exceed the mean wind speed by at least 10 knots.

Gusts at the ground are caused by either turbulence due to friction, wind shear or by solar heating of the ground. These three mechanisms can force the wind to quickly change speed as well as direction.
Gusts occur when turbulence briefly drags the stronger wind near the top of the friction layer down to the surface.
A squall is a sudden increase in wind speed which must meet three defined criteria:
1. The wind must reach a speed of at least 22 knots.
2. It must increase by at least 16kt, and
3. It must last for at least one minute.
Are rapid increases in wind speed which last for some minutes, then die away again.
Squalls are most often associated with passing Cumulonimbus (Cb) showers, or by the passage of frontal systems.
Often accompanied by thunderstorms and/or very heavy showers.
Marked changes in wind direction may also accompany squalls.

lessons.title: Diurnal Variation of the Surface Wind

content.content: During the day, the friction layer will be shallower and have less effect because the air is warm and less dense.
The wind will follow the isobars more closely and the strength will be similar to that above 2000 ft.
At night however, the air becomes dense, and the friction layer will thicken, the wind will flow slower and at an angle across the isobars.
This gives rise to the diurnal variation of the surface wind.
When we talk about wind direction change, it is referred to as veering or backing.
Veering
A clockwise change in wind direction.
Backing
An anticlockwise change in wind direction.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the surface wind backs and increases after daybreak.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the surface wind veers and decreases after sunset.

lessons.title: Wind Change During Climb or Descent

content.content: In the Southern Hemisphere, the wind backs and increases in a climb as the friction layer is vacated.
During a descent into the friction layer, the opposite holds true, the wind veers and decreases.
Measured by a cup anemometer consisting of three or four cups, conical or hemispherical in shape, mounted symmetrically about a vertical spindle 10m above the ground.
The wind blowing into the cups causes the spindle to rotate.
In standard instruments, the design of the cups is such that the rate of rotation is proportional to the speed of the wind to a sufficiently close approximation.

Wind direction is measured by a vane consisting of a thin horizontal arm carrying a vertical flat plate at one end with its edge to the wind, and at the other end, a balance weight which also serves as a pointer.
The arm is carried on a vertical spindle mounted on bearings which allow it to turn freely in the wind.
In reports or observations, wind speed = Kts, direction = Degrees True.
However, if you were given the wind by a pilot or controller, wind speed = Kts, but direction = Degrees Magnetic.
An approximation of wind speed and direction can be gained from this type of windsock.
You can also gauge the gustiness and the swing.
Wind ripples can give you an indication of the wind direction.
Wind lanes are streaks of disturbed water which flow with the wind.
They are often an indication of strong local winds.
The direction of the wind can be ascertained by the finger-like fraying at the downwind end.
Cloud shadows will drift and indicate wind aloft. The speed at which they are moving will also indicate how intense the upper-level wind velocity is.
Buys Ballot’s Law states:
If in the Southern Hemisphere, one stands with one’s back to the wind, the area of low pressure is to one’s right.
This has a practical application in that if you are flying toward a low-pressure area, and your altimeter is not adjusted, it will be over reading.
The speed and direction of the wind is not normally constant in either the vertical or horizontal plane.
If the change in speed or direction occurs over a shallow layer, windshear will be present.
The greater the change in wind speed or direction over the shallowest layer, the more severe the windshear will be.
If an aircraft descends through a shear zone below which the wind is lighter, the aircraft’s airspeed will decrease, its angle of descent will steepen, and the rate of descent will increase.
These changes can be brought under control but will require a certain amount of height to do so.
The greater the change in wind speed or direction over the narrower zone will make the windshear more severe.
Is a sudden increase in headwind, making the airspeed rise and making the aircraft fly above the glide slope.

If you expect positive wind-shear on final, you should land with a lower setting of flaps, giving more kinetic energy to the aircraft, increasing lift to drag ratio, and at the same time, increasing escape capability.
It also increases the approach speed, giving you more margin on stall.
The only negative issue that might be expected on landing with a lower setting of flaps, could be the runway length.
Is a sudden decrease in headwind, it doesn't necessarily need to be tailwind, but just an important drop in headwind, reducing the airspeed and making the aircraft fly below the glide slope.
If you are told you may encounter negative windshear on final, you should select a lower setting of flaps for the approach, for the same reasons that you did it on a positive windshear.
Tailwind approaches are performed much better with full flaps, but full flaps have a lower margin to go around if needed, and approach speeds have a lower stall margin than a lower setting of flaps.
Will need an increase in thrust in order to counteract the decrease in airspeed, but you will also need to be altitude-minded.
Anticipation is also the key here, do not let it diverge too much, and corrections will be smaller.
The sea breeze is caused by the land warming after sunrise while the sea remains at a constant temperature.
As the land warms, the air expands, and pressure drops off less quickly.
The result is that over the land at height, the pressure is higher than over the sea at the same height.
This upper air will start to flow in accordance with the pressure gradient.
As it does so, the pressure over the land falls, and rises over the sea, due to the transfer of mass.
This sets up a pressure gradient from the sea to land, and the sea breeze blows.
A sea breeze can form over any large water mass i.e., large lakes such as Lake Taupo.
Timing
In most cases the sea breeze sets in around 10am and peaks around 2–4 pm and continues to Sunset.
In tropical regions it can continue well after Sunset.
Strength
The strength is usually between 10 – 15 knots but depends on the temperature difference between land and sea, the greater the difference the stronger the breeze.
Horizontal and Vertical Extent
It can vary from place to place but generally it will extend 25–40 km inland and up to 2–3000 ft.
Cloud Formation
In gentle sea breeze situations, cloud will consist of a few cumulus clouds with some turbulence and reduced visibility from the land surface up to the cloud tops.
In tropical regions, the intense convection creates large cumulus build up and CBs.
Precipitation
Precipitation is not common except in tropical regions.
Temperature
The incoming cold sea air can cause a dramatic reduction in temperature, especially in Spring.
In Summer, the warmer sea reduces the temperature reduction.
Pressure Gradient
An intense sea breeze brings Coriolis force into play.
The flow over the land will turn cyclonic, and a heat low will develop.
This will turn the sea breeze across the coast.
Windshear
If the prevailing wind opposes the sea breeze, the sea breeze can slip in under the prevailing wind and cause a shear zone.
It can also cause a convergence type opposition; in this case, the surface wind can be very unpredictable.
Turbulence
The interference of sand dunes, hills, buildings etc. can cause moderate turbulence.
From the beach inland can be quite turbulent up to 2-3000 ft, but from the beach, out to sea and up will be very smooth.
Katabatic comes from the Greek word meaning ‘go down’.
In mountainous terrain, the valley floors tend to go into shadow quite early.
Therefore, the air cools and becomes denser and tends to flow down the valley.
Towards evening, when the valley walls also become subject to cooling, the air will cool, become dense and flow down the walls.
As the air descends, it is of course subject to adiabatic heating, however the continued flow of cold outweighs this effect.
In general, katabatic winds are light in strength and smooth.
If there is a river in the valley, the katabatic wind can bring additional cold air down and assist in the formation of valley fog.
Anabatic is the opposite to katabatic in that it means ‘go up’.
After Sunrise, valley walls are warmed by solar radiation.
Through conduction, the air touching the walls warm and will rise due to convection.
Replacement air is drawn up from the valley.
Rising air cools adiabatically and along with gravity, opposes the wind, which is therefore always fairly light.
The controlling factors for terrain channelling are:
Wind speed as a function of Pressure Gradient Force (PGF).
The steepness and proximity of adjacent high ground.
The stability of the atmosphere – a stable layer will enhance the effect.
Venturi Effect – think Cook Strait, Manawatu Gorge
Most real gap wind situations, where the strongest winds are generally over the exit region of the gap, not at the narrowest section or constriction.
No rigid lid in the real world. Airflow is not just through the gap formed by terrain but will flow over top as well.
With a stable layer of air above this will enhance the venturi effect.
In percentage terms, the atmosphere holds only small amounts of water.
The amount of atmospheric moisture depends largely on latitude, altitude and air temperature.
The oceans, with over 97% of the worlds water are the principal suppliers of atmospheric moisture.
The three most important processes in atmospheric moisture are:
Condensation
Evaporation
Precipitation

lessons.title: How much Water Vapour can a parcel of air hold?

content.content: 100% dry air
4% Water Vapour is all it can hold (100% Relative Humidity)
Condensation is the return of water vapour into liquid water, the main method being cooling of the atmosphere.
There are various methods by which this cooling can take place.
Condensation cannot take place without small solid particles for the water vapour to cling to.
These particles are called Condensation Nuclei (Aerosols).
If there is an over-abundance of condensation nuclei, the condensation process can be accelerated i.e., smog.
If there is a lack of condensation nuclei, then condensation may not occur at the temperature it should have, this is known as super-saturation.
Deposition is the process whereby water vapour molecules deposit directly into ice – the mechanism that builds ice on the walls of your freezer.
Evaporation is the change from liquid to gas.
The evaporation process requires latent heat.
The main factors which influence the rate of evaporation are:
Air Temperature
The greater the air temperature, the greater the rate of evaporation.
Water content of the air
The drier the air over the water surface, the greater the rate.
Wind
The stronger the wind, the greater the mixing of wet air with transported drier air, the greater the rate of evaporation.
Atmospheric Pressure
The lower the pressure, the greater the rate of evaporation.

Sublimation is a process where ice will change directly into water vapour, without going through the liquid state (in this case, dry ice, or frozen carbon dioxide, is sublimating directly to CO2 gas).
Transpiration is the process where plants absorb water through the roots and then give off water vapour through pores in their leaves.

Relative Humidity is the Ratio of the weight of the water vapour in a given quantity of air (absolute humidity) to the maximum weight of water vapour that the same volume could hold at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage.
The maximum weight of water vapour that the air could hold is called the saturation content.
The warmer the air, the greater the amount of water it can hold.
Relative Humidity is the relationship between water content and temperature.
If water is added, but the temperature remains the same, relative humidity rises.
If the water content remains constant but the temperature falls, relative humidity again rises.
Relative Humidity is not a measure of water content, a RH of 90% in the tropics is quite different to a RH of 90% in Polar regions.
As the diurnal variation of temperature takes place, so to does the diurnal variation of humidity.
Dew Point is the temperature at which a parcel of air saturates under constant pressure.
If a parcel of air is cooled to its Dew Point, and further cooling takes place, the water vapour that the air can no longer support will be transformed into liquid through the condensation process.
Dew point takes into consideration constant pressure, dew point will decrease by half a degree per thousand feet gained due to the reduction in pressure.
Dew point is not affected by a change in air temperature, the temperature that water will start condensing will remain constant.
Dew point is only affected by water content, if the water content is increased, the dew point value will be raised.
Relative Humidity is affected by changes in water content and temperature.
Dew Point is affected only by changes in water content (ignoring pressure).

The density of air (ρ) is the mass per unit volume of Earth's atmosphere. Air density, like air pressure, decreases with increasing altitude. It also changes with variation in temperature and humidity.
At sea level and at 15°C, air has a density of approximately 1.225 kg/m3.
Density is the term used to represent the number of molecules and how closely they are packed into any given volume of a substance.
The density of the surrounding air is the most important determinant of how well an aircraft and its engine can perform.
In a given parcel of air, there are countless millions of molecules.

They are in continuous motion, vibrating & moving at high speed at random. When they come close enough to a solid surface to collide with it, each molecule exerts a tiny pressure on that surface. Add them all up, and the total force can be quite considerable.

The amount of pressure exerted by air on a solid surface depends on the air’s density. The denser the air, the more molecules there are to collide with the surface to generate pressure. Hence pressure is a good indicator of density.
Temperature is a measure of how much energy the molecules of a substance have, i.e., how fast they vibrate.
If heat is transferred to air, the molecules become ‘excited’ its temperature will rise and with more kinetic energy, the force with which they collide with the surface will increase.
If the heated air is contained (in a box) its pressure will rise and fall as it cools.
If it’s not contained, its molecules with greater kinetic energy will move further apart and air will expand. With less molecules present than the original volume, its density will decrease.
To Summarise:
In different masses of air with the same temperature, the air with the highest pressure has the highest density.
In different masses of air with the same pressure, the air with the lowest temperature has the highest density.
As you move higher in the atmosphere, there's less air above you that can push on you.
As a result, air pressure decreases as you increase altitude, because there's less air pushing on it from above.
Likewise, the density of air also decreases, because it's not being squashed as hard as air below it.
The mass of a molecule of water vapour is less than the mass of a molecule dry air.
Thus, the density of moist air is less than the density of dry air.
There are three types of stability:
Stable
Unstable
Neutrally Stable
Air is stable if, after a disturbance it returns, or wants to return to its original position or height without any external force being applied.
Stable air will likely have fair to poor visibility.
If there is cloud it will be layer type.
Any precipitation will be drizzle or rain.
Air is unstable if, after a disturbance, it continues to move away from its original position or height.
Unstable air is characterised by cumulus type cloud.
Outside cloud visibility can be very good.
Precipitation will be showers, heavy at times.
Air is neutrally stable if, after a disturbance, it retains its new position without any tendency to return to its original position or deviate further.
Conditions are generally similar to stable air.
The temperature lapse rate that applies in each locality at a given time is known as the Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR).
It is a measure of the drop in temperature with height, note the air is not rising.
The ELR can be steep as in ‘a’.
Or can be shallow as in ‘e’.
It can show an inversion ‘b’.
It can show an isothermal layer ‘c’.
An adiabatic process (of temperature change) is one where no energy (heat) is gained from or lost to the surroundings.
As a parcel of air is made to rise, it enters heights where the atmospheric pressures are less and expands.
This expansions demands energy which is taken away from within the parcel in terms of temperature.
Thus, a rising parcel of air will cool adiabatically.
This rising parcel of air will cool at 3°C per 1000 ft.
The adiabatic process applies with descending air also, the air contracts and warms at 3°C/1000 ft.
This lapse rate applies, provided no water vapour condenses, the parcel must remain dry.
This is known as the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR).
The stability of air is dependent on the ELR and the adiabatic lapse rate.
If a parcel of air is forced to rise, it will cool at the DALR of 3°/1000ft.
The ELR will determine if the parcel of rising air is cooler or warmer than the surrounding air and determine its stability.
In this example, the rising parcel of air is colder than the surrounding air and will want to return to its original height, therefore it is Stable.
This graph illustrates the example and shows that with the DALR below the ELR, air is Stable.
In this example, the rising parcel of air is warmer than the surrounding air and will continue to rise, therefore it is Unstable.
This graph illustrates the example and shows that with the DALR above the ELR, air is Unstable.
When the DALR is greater than the ELR (the DALR lies below the ELR), then dry air is stable.
When the DALR is less than the ELR (the DALR lies above the ELR), then dry air is unstable.
As a parcel of air rises and cools, its relative humidity will increase.
RH will eventually become 100%, which is the Dew Point, condensation will take place, and latent heat will be released.
The latent heat causes heating and the adiabatic lapse rate changes from 3°C/1000ft to 1.5°C/1000 ft.
This is called the Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR).
The SALR tends to steepen with height, this is due to the limited amount of water vapour to release the latent heat of condensation.
As the water vapour starts running out, the SALR steepens.
The example shows a saturated parcel of air rising at the SALR, and is colder than the surrounding air, the parcel wants to return to its original height, therefore is Stable.
This graph illustrates the example and shows that with the SALR below the ELR, the air is Stable.
The example shows a saturated parcel of air rising at the SALR, that remains warmer than the surrounding air, the parcel wants to continue rising, therefore it is Unstable.
This graph illustrates the example and shows that with the SALR above the ELR, air is Unstable.
When the SALR is greater than the ELR (the SALR lies below the ELR), saturated air will be stable.
When the SALR is less than the ELR (the SALR lies above the ELR), saturated air will be unstable.
When the ELR is less than 1.5°C/1000 ft there will be Absolute Stability.
When the ELR is greater than 3°C/1000 ft there will be Absolute Instability.
When the ELR lies between the DALR and the SALR, we have Conditional Instability.
If the air is dry, it will be stable.
However, under the same conditions if the air is saturated, it will be unstable.
An ELR of 2°C/1000ft is the global norm, it is rare to have an ELR in excess of 3°C/1000ft and this is referred to as Super Adiabatic.

lessons.title: The Rising Condensation Level – Mechanical Rising

content.content: In the real-world, rising air will usually start off dry, then once it has cooled to dew point, it will be saturated.
It is possible to predict where cloud will start forming, the Rising Condensation Level (RCL), what type of cloud it will be and possibly where it will stop.
Cloud will form when the temperature meets the dew point.
As the air is always stable, the cloud will be layer type.
As the air is stable, the cloud will stop at the top of the hill.
The air is unstable from the start – therefore Cumulus cloud will form.
The cloud tops can be predicted in this case, because of the inversion.
In the second case, because the air is unstable, the cloud will continue to form.
The only way of predicting the tops, is if there is an inversion layer.
The cloud will stop forming if it runs out of moisture, this is not often the case and cannot be predicted.

lessons.title: The Convective Condensation Level – Thermal Rising

content.content: When the surface warms, the surrounding air will be warmed by conduction and convection.
If the warmed parcels of air remains warmer than the surrounding air, the air will rise.
It is possible to predict what level the cloud will form, the Convective Condensation Level.
Once again, the tops of the cloud cannot be predicted in the absence of an inversion.
For convective cloud to be produced, the DALR must meet the ELR before the dew point.
If the DALR meets the ELR before the dew point, the parcel of air and the surrounding air will be the same temperature and the air will stop rising and no cloud will form.

lessons.title: Required Surface Temperature for Convective Condensation Level

content.content: To calculate the minimum surface temperature to produce convective cloud, plot a vertical line up from the dew point (6°).
Where the ELR and this vertical line cross, note the height (5000ft).
Multiple this by 3 and add to the dew point value.
21°C is the minimum surface temp. for convective cloud to form in this example.
Initially, the 3000ft layer is absolutely unstable.
The ELR at the start is 4°C/1000ft (12° difference over 3000ft = 4°/1000ft).
Once the air has risen and cooled, the ELR has dropped to 1°/1000ft (3° difference over 3000ft = 1°/1000ft) and the air is stable (convective stability).
This refers to the behaviour of air as the surface temperature varies from day to night.
As the temperature increases after sunrise, the ELR steepens, and instability may occur.
The ELR will go through a phase where conditional stability exists.
In the afternoon, when the surface temperature peaks, the instability is at its maximum. The reverse happens at night.
The factors that affect surface temperature such as type of surface, latitude, season and cloud cover will strongly affect the degree of diurnal stability.
As has been stated, an inversion is a layer of air where the temperature increases instead of decreasing.
An inversion layer will cap any cloud, because it prevents the continuation of air rising.

Because the inversion layer caps the atmosphere, the visibility below the inversion can be poor, turbulence, wind and precipitation may take place, flying conditions above the inversion will be considerably better.
Moisture Content of air above an inversion is always less than that below it. Therefore, the dew point of the air above the inversion is lower than the dew point below.
Increased risk of carb icing below the inversion due to the increased moisture content of the air.

Since surface wind is calm or very light, takeoff or landing can be in any direction. Takeoff may be in the direction of the wind above the inversion. If so, the aircraft encounters a sudden tailwind and a corresponding loss of airspeed when climbing through the inversion. Stall is possible.
If approach is into wind above the inversion, the headwind is suddenly lost when descending through the inversion. Again, a sudden loss in airspeed may cause a stall.
Another important point to remember about inversions is that they invariably enhance stability of air.
Inversions are classified as:
Radiation inversion.
Turbulence inversion.
Subsidence inversion.
Frontal inversion.
Radiation inversions occur overnight in clear sky conditions.
The earth loses long-wave radiation to space at night, and thus it cools down.
The air in immediate contact with the cooling ground is also cooled by conduction and low-level mixing.
The cooled air may eventually reach 100 to 300 feet above the surface, with the coldest air remaining near the surface. This induces an inversion of the surface.
The temperature of the air above the inversion is not affected by surface cooling (air is a poor conductor), so it may be considerably warmer than the air at ground level.
Radiation fog and mist can only form in the presence of a radiation inversion.
Turbulence inversions are created at the top of the friction layer. They usually start with a uniform environmental temperature lapse rate of around 1 to 2 degrees Celsius per 1000ft.
Turbulence is induced within the friction layer by a wind of at least 10 knots blowing over surface obstacles like small hills, trees and buildings.
The depth of the turbulence and therefore the friction layer is determined by the roughness of the surface and the speed of the wind.
Turbulence inversions can occur at heights between about 1000 and 5000 feet, however they are most common at around 2000 to 3000 feet.

The air beneath the friction layer becomes turbulent (but mostly only light from an aviation perspective), and this tumbling motion means that some of the air is rising, and some is falling. The air that is rising is subjected to less pressure and so it expands and cools adiabatically.

The descending air is compressed and warmed adiabatically. The rising and falling air mixes with the environmental air. The cooling in the top half of the layer is offset by the warming in the bottom half of the layer.
A new ‘steeper’ lapse rate – one approximating the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate of 3°C per 1000 feet – is created.
The air above the friction layer is unaffected by the turbulence below, and so it remains warmer than the induced cooling beneath the newly created inversion.

If sufficient moisture is present for the cooling to reach saturation point, Stratocumulus cloud is produced with the tops capped by the top of the inversion. Sc is a cloud induced by turbulence in this case.
Subsidence inversions have their roots in the upper Troposphere during the initial formation process of a developing surface high pressure area.
High-level air just beneath the Tropopause converges and begins to sink and, as more air converges into the same area, the surface pressure starts to rise.
The sinking air is subjected to increasing pressure and is therefore compressed, and so it warms adiabatically. A subsidence inversion is first created in the mid-Troposphere.

As the air continues to descend, the inversion develops and becomes stronger. The descent usually stops somewhere between 3,000 and 8,000ft above MSL, where it meets weak convective currents rising of the surface.
The sinking air above a subsidence inversion originates in the upper Troposphere, where the air is very dry and typically cloud-free.

If you fly up through one of these inversions, there will be a very marked decrease in relative humidity and dew point as you do so, and consequently, there is likely to be very little cloud, if any, above a subsidence inversion.
A frontal inversion occurs at any frontal surface when warm air is forced to rise over the top of a layer of colder air.

The height at which the inversion is intercepted depends on your position relative to the surface position of the front. Closer to this position and the inversion will be lower; further away and the inversion will be higher.
In radiation, turbulence and subsidence inversions, the atmosphere tends to ‘dry out’ above the inversion.

Frontal inversions are different in that the air temperature and the dew point temperature will remain close together through the inversion because the cloud layer will often be continuous through this area, with heavy rain falling through it.
Turbulent mixing within the friction layer which can create an inversion, usually at a height of between 3000ft and 5000ft.
If sufficient moisture is available just beneath the inversion, Stratocumulus (Sc) cloud may form. This type of cloud is Stratocumulus formed by turbulence.
The second process involves a developing Cumuliform cloud that, on reaching a strong inversion, stops growing or, on reaching a weak inversion, punches through it and continues to grow vertically.
In either case, Sc cloud will spread out horizontally beneath the inversion.
Very low-level cloud and/or fog often require the development of a radiation inversion to form.
Such inversions develop of the surface and so the moisture is trapped at very low levels.
Layered cloud found at higher levels in the Troposphere is also often associated with weak inversions.
Inversions act like a blanket to trap low-level pollutants, especially around towns and cities or industrial areas, and near the coast on windy days.
Consequently, visibility beneath an inversion can be substantially reduced.
It is not uncommon to have 100km plus visibility above the inversion but have only 10 – 20km visibility below.
Beneath an inversion, light mechanical turbulence is common.
Just below the top of the inversion, the turbulence may become moderate as the fast-moving laminar air above the inversion interacts with the slower moving air beneath, creating windshear.
Above the inversion, the turbulence will cease, even though the wind speeds will almost certainly be higher than at lower levels.
Inversions cap most of the vertical transport of moisture from the Earth’s surface.
This means that, assuming no other factors are at play, the water vapour content of this air will slowly increase over time, and so will the dew point temperature.
The relative humidity may or may not increase, depending on the temperature of the air beneath the inversion.
Dew point is less above inversion.
Not only does the risk of carburettor icing increase in an inversion, but the severity is likely to increase slightly as well.
This is simply because the air beneath the inversion traps increasing amounts of water vapour.

As the pressure in the carburettor venturi decreases and the air rapidly cools, the air containing a higher water vapour content will more readily form ice if the temperature falls below 0°C within the barrel.
Inversions enhance the effect of windshear by separating the faster moving air above the inversion from the slower moving air beneath.
Thus, inversions are almost always associated with turbulence due to windshear.
When inversions occur close to the ground, the risk posed by this windshear increases.
Most aircraft will experience some degradation in performance when passing through an inversion.
Some light aircraft, particularly some 4 or 6 seaters, are quite under-powered for the tasks they are often called upon to perform.
An aircraft that is loaded full of people and fuel (but still within the performance envelope for take-off) may well struggle to climb through an inversion.
This is because the air within the inversion is considerably less dense than the air was at take-off due to the combined effects of increasing temperature and lowering pressure.
In simple terms, cloud is suspended water in liquid droplet or ice crystal form.
Remember that for the condensation process to take place, condensation nuclei are required.
There are by far, more condensation nuclei over the land than sea.
For condensation to take place, the air must be brought to 100% relative humidity.
Relative Humidity can be raised by increasing the water content or by reducing the temperature.

The most common method through which RH is raised, is by cooling of the air and in turn the most common method of achieving the cooling is through the ascent of air allowing the adiabatic process to cool the air.

Modern cloud ceilometers fire a low-powered laser beam upward. The beam bounces off the base of a cloud layer back to the ground unit and, through simple mathematics, calculates the height of the layer.
A portion of the beam will also pass through the lowest layer and bounce off a higher layer, so multiple layers can be scanned.
They operate by day and at night.

In terms of cloud amounts, the sensor measures the time it records a base versus the time it doesn’t for the same height, so for example, if it registers cloud at say 1500 feet for 50% of the time, there is an estimated 4/8ths of cloud in the layer, reported as SCT.

The system is very accurate at measuring cloud bases immediately above the sensor. The cloud reported in the observation will only be accurate in cases where the cloud is moving across the sensor in clumps, or in an overcast situation.
There are limitations however, and these are:
The sensor only samples cloud that passes immediately above, so distant clouds are missed.
A small patch of stationary cloud immediately above the sensor will be reported as an overcast layer when the sky may be far from overcast.
Approaching low cloud will be missed until it is immediately over the sensor.
An overcast layer with a hole immediately above the sensor may be recorded as NCD – No Cloud Detected.

Finally, the sensor cannot differentiate between cloud types, thus /// is included after every cloud group to indicate that the cloud could be either TCu or Cb. Note that in some instances, it is easy to estimate what the cloud type should be. For example, a layer reported as OVC for several hours must be layer cloud – Sc or St. It cannot be TCu or Cb.
The methods by which air can rise are:
Convective rising (Thermal).
Orographic rising – large scale (Mountains).
Mechanical rising – small scale ( Hills, ranges).
Frontal lifting – (Cold/Warm fronts).
Surface convergence – (low Pressure).
Wave action lifting.
The type of cloud that forms is dependent on the stability of the air.
Orographic Cloud – Stable Conditions
Orographic Cloud Forming in Unstable Conditions

If the air is stable and precipitation occurs, the air will descend on the Lee side and the cloud base will be higher than on the windward side and this will generate warmer surface temperature – the Föhn Effect.
Convective lifting results when low-level air is heated, e.g. when land is heated directly by solar radiation, or when a cold outbreak of air moves over a warmer sea.
The air in contact with this warmer surface is heated by conduction and therefore becomes lighter than the air surrounding it, and so rises spontaneously due to its own internal buoyancy.
Thermals are areas where convection is occurring.

But the air is very dry, and so the thermal has not been able to rise high enough to create enough internal cooling (through the adiabatic process) for the parcel to become saturated, and therefore cloud has not formed.
Turbulence describes the process whereby air tumbles over obstacles like buildings, trees and smaller hills and bluffs.
The mechanical nature of the tumbling creates an overturning motion, with some of the air rising and thus cooling.
If the low-level atmosphere is stable and sufficient lifting occurs for the air to become saturated, then cloud will form.

At a front, there is widespread lifting of air as warm air comes into contact with colder air. Layer type clouds form in the stable air at a warm front and heap clouds in the unstable air at a cold front.
The Formation of Frontal Cloud
Once cloud has formed, it may simply stay there, or precipitation may take place.
If precipitation does not take place, the water drops must be held up by sufficiently strong up currents, this is referred to as the air’s buoyancy.
Buoyancy is enhanced by convection and the forced ascent such as orographic lifting.
Although not always visible, large numbers of water drops fall from cloud but evaporate before reaching the ground.
The factors that affect the rate of this evaporation are:
The relative humidity of the air below the cloud.
The state of the falling water i.e., liquid or solid.
The size of the drop.
The Internationally adopted system classifies cloud under the following characteristics:
Shape and structure.
Vertical extent.
Altitude.
As most of the cloud is contained in the Troposphere, and the height of the Tropopause varies with latitude, cloud classification by altitude must reflect this.
High Cloud
Tropical Latitudes
6 km and higher, 20,000 ft and higher.
Mid Latitudes
5 km and higher, 17,000 ft and higher.
Middle Cloud
Tropical Latitudes
Between 2 – 6 km, 7 – 20,000 ft
Mid Latitudes
Between 2 – 5 km, 7 – 17,000ft
Low Cloud
Tropical Latitudes
Below 2km, Below 7,000ft.
Mid Latitudes
Below 2km, Below 7,000ft.
High Cloud
Cirrostratus(CS)
Smooth and fibrous appearance.
Can cover large areas of sky.
Often is an indication of approaching deteriorating weather.
Turbulence not associated with CS.
Cirrocumulus(CC)
Has a cotton wool appearance.
Can almost cover the entire sky or just small areas. Minimal turbulence.
Cirrus(CI)
Feather-like type of cloud.
Covers less than the total sky. Can indicate high wind speeds aloft which causes a streaky appearance. Turbulence light to moderate.
With these three types of cloud (CS, CC, CI) icing problems are remote, despite very cold temperatures found at the altitudes involved.
There is no precipitation from these clouds.
Middle Cloud
Altostratus(AS)
Often covers extensive areas across the sky.
Is often an indication of approaching deteriorating weather.
Has a blue/gray appearance. AS can have extensive depth and due to this, icing can be severe, especially if the freezing level lies within.
Precipitation at sea level is usually light, but in mountainous terrain may be moderate to heavy. Turbulence is not usually present.
Altocumulus (AC)
Appears as a layer of patches of cloud.
Turbulence can be moderate if associated with active fronts, orographic rising of unstable air, but otherwise is light.
Icing can occur if cloud water content is high and depends on the latitude and type of terrain over which cloud has formed. Precipitation is not common.
Low Cloud
Stratocumulus (SC) appears as a layer or patch composed of globular masses or rolls.
SC may cover large parts of the sky. Turbulence will be light.
Icing is not considered a problem except when the Freezing Level (FZL) is close to the ground.
Precipitation may be light showers or drizzle.
Stratus (ST)
Shallow layer of cloud resembling fog but with its base above ground level.
Turbulence not associated with ST.
Icing will be light if (FZL) is at ground level. Light drizzle may occur.
Cumulus (CU)
Heaped cloud type with sharp outlines and vertical development. The upper surface is dome shaped and the base nearly flat.
Precipitation is unusual but if development is substantial, brief showers may occur.
Turbulence is likely within the cloud and outside it. Icing is not a problem due to fragmented nature of the cloud.
Cumulonimbus (CB)
Cloud with great vertical development. Easily identified by an anvil like structure at the top of the cloud.
Turbulence can be moderate to severe, depending on development.
Icing is also a serious problem with both forms occurring.
Heavy shower activity can take place and may include hail.
Nimbostratus (NS)
Low shapeless layer of dark grey cloud of nearly uniform appearance.
Usually, no turbulence unless an embedded Cb is within.
Precipitation is steady and persistent and can be accompanied by snow and sleet. Rime ice is common, and it is possible to experience clear ice.
Stable moist air flows over a mountain or a range of mountains, a series of large-scale standing waves may form on the downwind side.
If the temperature at the crest of the wave drops to the dew point, moisture in the air may condense to form lenticular clouds.
As the moist air moves back down into the trough of the wave, the cloud may evaporate back into vapour.
Under certain conditions, long strings of lenticular clouds can form near the crest of each successive wave, creating a formation known as a “wave cloud”.
Avoid flying near lenticular clouds because of the turbulence of the rotor systems that accompany them.
A rotor (cloud) is a closed, vertical circulation that develops in the lee of high mountain barriers, or in the valley between two mountain ranges, when conditions are appropriate.
The rotor is a form of lee eddy. At the surface, the wind is in the opposite direction to the gradient wind.
Rotors are often associated with extreme turbulence and are often marked by a rotor cloud such as the helm bar.
Means divisions of eighths and is how cloud coverage is referred to.
Cloud Amounts
Sky Clear(SKC), means no cloud.
Few(FEW), means a cloud coverage of 1 to 2 oktas.
Scattered(SCT), means a cloud coverage of 3 to 4 oktas.
Broken(BKN) refers to a cloud cover between 5 and 7 oktas.
Overcast(OVC) means the sky is covered by 8 oktas of cloud.
Lowest layer of cloud is always reported .
The cloud layer above is reported if it is 3 oktas or more.
The highest layer of cloud is reported if it is 5 or more oktas.
If Cbs or TCus are detected, they may replace some of these.
Determining Cloud Heights
Searchlight- A light is shone vertically onto the base of the cloud and using an alidade and calculation tables cloud height is determined.
Sinking of air In regions where air is subsiding, the temperature is increasing because the pressure is also increasing.
Subsidence is found in anticyclones and in small areas adjacent to cumuliform clouds. Descending air is also found on the downwind side of wave crests.
Mixing with clear air The mixing of saturated air with drier air near cumulus tops leads to evaporation of the cloud droplets.
Evaporation cools the air and therefore it begins to sink.
Sinking warms the air, and so further evaporation takes place.
Direct warming Often during the afternoon, the temperature at ground level increases, but the dew point remains the same.
As the temperature and dew point separate, the cloud base rises and eventually the bases may reach the level of the cloud tops causing the cloud to dissipate completely from the bottom up.
Cloud Dispersal
The main cause is adiabatic warming. The cloud sinks, warms up above the dew point and evaporation takes place and the cloud dissipates.
In meteorology, precipitation is any product of the condensation of atmospheric water vapour that falls under gravity.
The main forms of precipitation include drizzle, rain, sleet, snow, and hail.

Precipitation occurs when a portion of the atmosphere becomes saturated with water vapour, so that the water condenses and "precipitates". Thus, fog and mist are not precipitation but suspensions, because the water vapour does not condense sufficiently to precipitate.
Bergeron Process
Ice crystals are formed by deposition, they then increase in size by collision and bonding to water droplets.
This occurs above the freezing layer, where water vapour is supercooled.
Requires freezing Nuclei – solid particles that have a crystal form closely resembling ice.
Freezing nuclei are sparse, do not become active till -10°C.
Once the ice crystals are too heavy, they fall to the surface.
Air must become saturated (100% R/H), below -10°C when Ice crystals start forming, it becomes supersaturated.
Ice crystals will come in contact with supercooled water vapour and grow.
They continue to enlarge though collision with larger super cooled drops.
Some crystals will break up and become freezing nuclei themselves.
When they are large enough, they will fall.
The state of the precipitation depends on the temperature of the lower atmosphere.
Occurs In warm clouds, where all of the cloud droplets are liquid.
The collision-coalescence process is the primary mechanism responsible for producing precipitation.
Cloud droplets collide and coalesce or stick together.
Larger cloud droplets have slightly higher terminal velocities, because they have a smaller surface-area-to-weight ratios.
This advantage allows them to fall faster and collide with smaller cloud droplets.
Sometimes the cloud droplets will stick together and coalesce to form a larger droplet.
These larger droplets then fall even faster, collide with even more smaller droplets in their path, and aggregate more and more cloud droplets together.
However, collision between cloud droplets does not always mean that coalescence will occur.
Sometimes droplets will bounce apart during collision if their surface tensions are too strong.
For collision-coalescence to begin, a cloud needs to have a wide distribution of cloud droplet sizes.
Virga are trails of precipitation that fall from the underside of a cloud but evaporate or sublime before it can reach the Earth's surface.
This happens when falling rain or ice passes through an area of dry or warm air.
Rate Of Fall Of Water Drops
Largely depends on the size of the water drops. The bigger they are, the faster they fall.
Other factors include gravity and drag on the drop itself.
Types Of Precipitation
Rain (RA) - most common type of precipitation and have a diameter of greater than 0.5mm.
Drizzle (DZ)- lightest form of precipitation in diameter. Made up of fine water droplets 0.5mm or less.
Snow (SN) - are branched or star-shaped ice crystals.
Sleet (RASN, SNRA) - is a combination of snow and rain.
Hail (GS or GR) - made up of both rime and clear ice.
Vary in size from 3mm radius to 40mm radius and larger in extreme cases.
Character Of Precipitation
Continuous Precipitation- which is not likely to clear in the short term.
Intermittent Precipitation- periods of rain, drizzle or snow with temporary improvements but with precipitation returning.
Showers of Precipitation- small bursts of precipitation then clearing.
Rate of Precipitation
The rate of precipitation is determined by the amount of water falling on a flat surface or into a rain gauge per unit time.
The rate of precipitation is determined by the amount of water falling on a flat surface or into a rain gauge per unit time.
Light (-) Between a trace of rain and < 2.5mm per hour.
Moderate > 2.5mm/hour < = 10mm/hour.
Heavy (+) > 10mm/hour
Visibility
The ability to see through air.
Visibility is determined by the transparency of the air.
When you have rain, drizzle, dust or smoke in the air, transparency is poor therefore visibility is poor also. When the air is clear, transparency will be good therefore visibility will be good.
The Sun and moon have no effect on visibility as it relates only to the transparency of the air.
Visibility Distance
Precipitation
Rain Heavy(+)- can relate visibility to less than 500 metres.
Moderate - reduces visibility to between 4-10 kilometres
Light(-) - has a limited effect on visibility, can exceed 20km.
The effect of drizzle or snow differs from rain because both reflect more light which causes a further reduction in visibility.
Snow and sleet can also be associated with Cbs, where such precipitation occurs in the form of showers.
DZ or Snow Intensity: Visibility:
Light 8,000 metres or more.
Moderate less than 8,000 metres but more than 500m.
Heavy less than 500m.
The visibility in fog and mist is a function of how many water droplets there are in suspension in the atmosphere, and therefore how much light scatter there is.
In all other respects, the make-up and formation processes are the same.
The difference comes down to one of actual visibility reduction caused.
Fog- cloud on the surface, vis will reduce to less than 1000 metres.
Mist- is reported when the vis is 1000 metres or more but does not exceed 5000 metres.
Haze is solid particles of dust, smoke, and other chemical pollutants in suspension in the atmosphere.
To be reported in a METAR, the visibility in haze and/or smoke must reduce visibility considerably.
Visibility reductions due to haze and smoke are made considerably worse by the presence of a low-level inversion.
Visibility: Haze (HZ) & Smoke (FU) ≤ 5,000 metres.
