In rough sea conditions, breaking waves result in very small sea water droplets being thrown up into the air.
Droplets get caught in the turbulent air above the waves and tumble about rather than returning to the sea surface.
The water quickly evaporates, leaving behind minute particles of sea salt.
The worst visibilities will be along the shore-line where the waves are breaking.
In extremely rough sea states, visibility reductions to perhaps 10km have been observed many kilometres inland.

Another problem associated with sea salt aerosols is that they stick to all surfaces they touch; especially aircraft windscreens where they will form an oily sheen which can further reduce visibility.
Sea salt aerosols are by far the most numerous of all condensation nuclei in the atmosphere.
Visibility reductions in blowing snow can be extremely poor and flying on instruments within the effected layer will be a necessity.
Blowing snow, or ‘blizzards’, is caused by wind lifting snow of the surface.
Just how high the snow is lifted is a function of wind speed, snow state (wet or dry), and stability within the lower atmosphere.
Generally, immediately above a snow-covered surface, a very low-level inversion will exist. This limits the height to which the snow is lifted to the lowest 100 feet or so.
For new, dry snow, a 10-knot wind will often be enough to cause visibility reductions to almost zero within the lowest 20 feet or so.
Old or wet snow may require up to 40 knots to achieve the same result.
Blowing snow should not be confused with flight through a heavy snowstorm. With the former, the very poor visibility is confined to a shallow layer immediately above the surface.
Visibility above blowing snow will generally be good. The poor visibility associated with flight through a heavy snowstorm will be extremely poor through a great of perhaps 20,000 feet or more.
Drifting Snow
Drifting snow is only raised from the ground surface by the wind to a height of less than 2 m (6 ft) creeping, rolling and bouncing above the surface.
While drifting snow is not regarded as a vision hazard for aviation, it is a major hazard for surface transportation.
Sun Glare
Can make landing and takeoff difficult. At times completely blinding you.
Happens when light reflects off objects e.g., the nose cowling. Also, when the Sun is low in the sky(morning or evening).
Possible flicker vertigo due to prop.
Difficult to judge distances and pick out objects or shapes.
Visibility Range
Colour Background - can occasionally totally obliterate one’s ability to see individual objects.
White-out conditions, when flying towards snow covered hills, these can be invisible if the background is also white.

Sunlight/Moonlight- when looking into the Sun, you cannot see an object as well when compared to looking down Sun. It’s the opposite for moonlight, you can see further and more clearly looking into the moon.
Slant Range
When flying directly overhead an airport, slant range is not a problem.
But when on approach because you have a longer distance to look through the haze layer, visibility rapidly deteriorates.
Runway Visual Range
RVR is usually given to pilots when visibility falls below 1500 metres.
Two methods are used, one with an observer using pre-determined objects at varying distances, or by using transmissometers.
Altitude And Visibility
At altitude, the air is almost clear of dust, haze and cloud.
Due to the absence of these matters, the human eye finds it difficult to focus, and see objects, like other aircraft.
Handar Visibility Sensor
The sensor sends out an infrared beam, while the receiver detects radiation which is scattered in the vicinity. This information is converted into a visibility range in kms.
The visibility sensors used in AWS are called ‘Forward Scatter Meters.
They fire out a beam of infrared light which is scattered by minute particles floating in the air.

Some of the light beam will be scattered into the receiver about half a metre away. From the amount of scatter received, the instrument can measure the turbidity of the air, and then calculate the horizontal visibility by extrapolation.
They operate by day or night.
The visibility is only sampled near the sensor; therefore, the limitations are:

The prevailing visibility may be much better than reported if there is localised mist or fog near the sensor only. In such situations, it would be useful to view a sequence of recent reports rather than one routine report in isolation.
The prevailing visibility may be very poor in some areas around the aerodrome if fog has formed over the airfield but not near the sensor.
Approaching poor visibility associated with an isolated shower, or rain with a front will not be measured until it reaches the sensor.
The sensor cannot determine directions where there are significant visibility variations.
Most of the MetService visibility sensors are limited to reporting visibility up to 20km only. Thus, when visibility is reported as 20km, it could be considerably better than that.

Fog comes in several different forms, but each relies on the air at ground or sea-level being cooled from below to the point of saturation, at which point condensation occurs. The different types of fog are as follows:
Radiation fog: Caused by the Earth cooling at night due to the loss of terrestrial radiation to space.
Advection fog: Caused by moist air from the sub-tropics moving South over colder waters and being cooled from below.

Steam fog: Formed when cold air moves over warm water. The high rate of evaporation from the water quickly saturates the cold air above, and wispy fog forms. This form of fog is rarely a problem to aviation.

Frontal fog: When there is a prolonged period of rain associated with a warm front, the air near the ground can become saturated due to the rain evaporating into it. Effectively, the cloud base continues to lower to ground level as the frontal surface approaches.
Upslope fog: This is simply the cloud formation process, it is low-level stratus (St) cloud, however if you are on the side of the hill above the cloud base, you are effectively within a fog layer.
If the sky is clear at night, the Earth’s heat is radiated out into space as long-wave radiation.
The ground cools, and the air in contact with the ground also cools through conduction.
This cooling process slowly spreads upwards through the lower layers of the atmosphere.
If the sky remains clear (so that cooling continues) and the air is sufficiently moist, then condensation eventually takes place.

In calm conditions, the cooling affects only a very shallow layer near the ground and so only dew or frost will form. However, with a slight breeze of 3 to 8 knots, the air is mixed a little and therefore cooled through a deeper layer up to 300ft above the ground.
The updraughts also help in keeping the water droplets suspended in the air.
Radiation fog only forms over land; however, this will include mud flats if the tide is out.
Once formed, radiation fogs may drift out over harbours and estuaries. If the surface wind is stronger than about 7-8 knots, the depth of the friction layer is increased.
This mixes warmer, drier air from near the top of the inversion down to the surface, effectively lowering the relative humidity and stopping the fog from forming.
If radiation fog has formed and the wind then increases, it will clear through the same process.
For advection fogs to form in the Southern Hemisphere, the air must have a northerly component to it – bringing warm moist air from the sub-tropics, progressively becoming stable.
If it is cooled to its dew point over a depth of a few hundred feet, typically requiring at least a few days, then fog will form.

The formation conditions (related to cloud cover, location, time of day, humidity near the surface and wind) are described below, but some of the points listed are not in fact restrictions at all; they are given for simple comparison purposes.
Advection fog forms:
In clear or cloudy skies.
Over land or sea.
At any time of day or night.
With high humidity near the ground.
In all wind speeds, up to 20 - 25 knots.
Advection fog is much more persistent than radiation fog and may last for days.
Advection Fog
In most cases, the clearance of advection fog occurs when there is a complete change in airmass i.e. a front passes through the area followed by a drier airmass.
In rare circumstances, the sun may warm the air enough to cause the water droplets to evaporate.
Once formed, the fog will persist even if the wind increases to storm force, so long as the wind direction and original airmass is maintained.
Serious reduction of visibility with fog (sometimes to less than 100m).
Affects take-offs and landings.
While in flight, fog is not a problem since it is rarely more than a few hundred feet thick.
It can become quite widespread at times, limiting the number of usable airfields, so caution should be exercised.
Fog may occur in any season of the year if the formation conditions are met but is most frequent from late Autumn to early Spring.
Katabatic winds flow down valleys, so if radiation fog is to form in a valley, the katabatic flow must be no more than the 7-8 knots allowable in the radiation fog formation process.
Radiation fog is very much influenced by topography, and valleys often have a ready supply of moisture and light katabatic winds flowing down them, enhancing the likelihood of fog forming.
If the valley system is big enough however – like the Rangitikei river valley for example – the katabatic wind may become too strong and kill any chance of fog formation.
The hazards are:
Decreased lift
Decreased thrust
Increased weight
Increased drag
Tail plane stalling (in most cases before the main plane)
Main plane stalling
Damage to trailing surfaces from blocks of ice falling of forward surfaces
Ice ingestion into engines, causing damage
Intake icing
Propeller icing
High-altitude ice crystals may cause a loss of power in jet engines
Gear doors frozen shut
Control surfaces freezing solid
Uncommanded full deflection of control surfaces
Uneven ice distribution leading to severe vibration and structural failure
Poor radio reception due ice build-up on aerials
Poor visibility due icing on wind-screens
Pitot tube and static vents icing over
Clear Ice
When Supercooled Water Droplets (SCWD) strike the aircraft, they don’t freeze instantly. Some of the water flows back over the aircraft. Forms in temperatures between 0° & -15°C.
This causes the air bubbles to be squeezed out resulting in a solid sheet of glass-like ice covering the wing.
Dangers Of Clear Ice
It can spread to parts that don’t have de-icing equipment.
Clear ice can flow over a hinge line of a control, freezing it in place.
If it begins to break up, it can do so in large parts and if they strike the aircraft, they will cause damage.
Rime Ice
With rime ice, the water freezes a lot quicker. Forms when temperature of the droplet is colder than -15°C.
This causes pockets of air to be trapped within it, giving it a milky opaque appearance.
Rime ice is rough and uneven in shape.
Dangers With Rime Ice
Forms on leading edges, and if not picked up early can greatly alter aerodynamic performance.
Hoar frost forms mostly on aircraft parked outside on a cold Winter’s night, however it can also form in flight.
The night-time/early morning hoar frost is simply a function of the land and adjacent surfaces (such as parked aircraft) radiating heat to space on a clear night.

This causes the land and the surfaces to cool to sub-zero temperatures. Any dew on the aircraft then freezes and the process of deposition then continues to build ice crystals directly onto the skin of the aircraft as frost (not just on the wings, but all over).
NOTE: This type of icing is extremely dangerous if not properly removed before flight is attempted.
Hoar frost in flight occurs when an aircraft is initially flown in temperatures colder than 0°C for a period, such that the skin of the aircraft cools to temperatures colder than zero.
If the aircraft then descends into cloud, or even into air beneath the freezing level with a high relative humidity, hoar frost will form quickly on the aircraft skin.
This form of hoar frost is not normally dangerous as it melts very quickly.
However, if the freezing level is very low and it forms on the windscreen, it may reduce the pilot’s visibility to zero at a crucial stage during the approach.
Delay take-off until the ice has fully melted naturally. This will work but your departure may be delayed for several hours.

Use a stiff broom to brush the worst of the ice off. This works but may damage the aircraft paint scheme. At times, a thick layer of dew may form on the aircraft before freezing takes place. This ice cannot be removed by brushing the aircraft.
Spray the aircraft with a de-icing fluid, usually propylene glycol fluid. It works well, but it is expensive, and it’s unlikely you can access it easily anyway.
Spraying the aircraft with water from a garden hose.
If you can spray water on the aircraft, keep spraying the entire aircraft until the whole skin has warmed to the temperature of the tap water.

Having done this, you should then endeavour to get airborne as soon as possible or you may inadvertently end up with a worse icing problem as water on the aircraft skin and trapped in control surfaces etc. may, within 15 to 30 minutes, freeze in the sub-zero air.
Freezing Rain
When you have a layer of warmer air above a layer of air less than 0 degrees and rain falls through this layer, freezing rain can occur.
If freezing rain is encountered, it is best to get out of the area is quickly as possible.
Snow encountered during flight will tend to swirl around the aircraft.
It will accumulate against objects where it can become trapped – under the windscreen wipers for example – however the biggest threat in flight is the very poor visibility it creates.
Snow on the aircraft while parked on the ground is another matter altogether. Think about the weight on the aircraft.
It should be fully removed before flight is attempted.

Sleet will tend to stick to the aircraft in flight; however, the problem is not that serious because sleet, by its very nature, is only found beneath the freezing level in air that is a degree or two warmer than zero Celsius.
Consequently, if possible, descent by perhaps 500ft, should get you below the sleet level.

If, however, you cannot descend, or you elect to continue flight in sleet conditions, the build-up of slushy ice on the leading edge of the wing will cause the stall speed to slowly rise, and as you slow the aircraft on approach, a fully developed stall is a distinct possibility.
Hail can cause serious damage to aircraft in flight or on the ground.
In flight, medium sized hail (bigger than perhaps 10 – 15mm) will cause dents on leading edges.
Hailstones bigger than about 20mm, will cause large dents on wings and spinners, and may crack windscreens.
Aircraft parked outside in large hail will also be severely dented, and large hail will pass right through fabric-covered aircraft like Tiger Moths, necessitating a complete re-skin of the aircraft.
Water content within clouds greatly affects accretion rates. Clouds form when the relative humidity is 100%.
Warm air can hold more moisture than cold air, so when flying through cloud in warm temps above the freezing level, ice can build up very quickly.
Sharp aircraft components tend to encourage ice buildup quicker than blunt parts due to compression.
Areas like aerials, fins, propellers and wings, depending on the shape of the leading edge, are the first places to experience ice.
Aerosols are an important ingredient in the development of cloud. Inside every cloud droplet (and there are billions of them), there is an aerosol.
Aerosols come in two forms: Condensation nuclei and Freezing nuclei. Below the freezing level, in temperatures greater than 0°C, every cloud droplet must contain a condensation nucleus.
If we were to lift these droplets above the freezing level (into an environment where temperatures may be significantly colder than 0°C), we would expect the droplet to freeze.
But this doesn’t happen automatically. Unless the droplet contains a suitable freezing nucleus, it will remain liquid. These liquid water droplets are called ‘Super-Cooled Water Droplets’ or ‘SCWD’.

As the SCWDs continue to rise into progressively colder air, they will eventually reach a temperature at which the internal aerosol ‘switches’ from being a condensation nucleus to a freezing nucleus, and at that point, the droplet will freeze.

The temperature at which this happens depends on the crystalline nature of the aerosol. By the time the air temperature has cooled to -40°C, all the condensation nuclei will have switched to become freezing nuclei.
Your aircraft is an amazingly good freezing nucleus. When SCWD collide with your aircraft, they will freeze to the airframe on contact.
All cloud immediately above the freezing level has the potential to create an airframe icing problem.

This is especially true if forced lifting has occurred i.e. in TCu, Cb and the up-drafting portion of some AC Lenticularis cloud. Flight into cloud above the freezing level exposes your aircraft to any of the potential hazards previously listed.
In Summary - If you're in visible moisture (cloud or rain) above the freezing level, expect to get icing.
The answer to this objective is simple – avoid flight in all cloud types above the freezing level.

If you do decide to undertake flight in cloud, and you observe ice forming anywhere on the airframe during flight, get out of the cloud immediately, or descend below the freezing level immediately if possible.
Carburettor ice occurs because of two processes.
When air is depressurised, the temperature is reduced and when fuel vaporises, the temperature reduces due to the requirement for latent heat.
When air enters the carburettor, it can cool below 0 degrees and any moisture present inside will turn into ice.
Carburettor ice can occur with an outside temperature between +25/-15 degrees.
Common method used to clear carburettor ice is carburettor heat.
This is hot air ducted from the exhaust manifold.
Throttle Plate
Moisture Content
The higher the moisture content of the air, the more likely it is that serious carburettor icing will form. This is because the high-water vapour content provides plenty of moisture to form ice.
Temperature
If the temperature within the carburettor barrel is capable of being cooled by up to 30°C, the outside air temperature (OAT) need not be close to zero degrees for carburettor icing to occur.

In fact, warmer sub-tropical air can have a high-water vapour content (temperature/dew point close together, 23°/20° for example), meaning carburettor icing is more likely to form at higher temperatures than at quite low temperatures, where there is limited water vapour available.
Temperature Gradient
Inversions occur when warm, and often moist air overlies cold, relatively dry air.
Therefore, flight immediately above the inversion is more prone to icing than flight below it.

lessons.title: Accretion Rate of Carburettor Ice Ice
Factors Affecting Carburettor Ice On the Ground

content.content: When on the ground at idle power settings, carburettor icing is a serious problem.
With the throttle closed, the risk of ice jamming the butterfly shut is high.
For this reason, we apply carburettor heat to melt any ice prior to takeoff.
Carburettor heat is unfiltered warm air extracted from around the exhaust system.
This heated air is less dense than the ambient air, and so there will be a noticeable drop in RPM.
But being unfiltered, means there is a risk of introducing dust and seeds etc. into the carburettor and engine.
These may ultimately lead to an engine failure after takeoff.
Aircraft which are used frequently from grass strips should be kept clean in the engine bay to avoid exacerbating this potential problem.
Light – Minor coverage of aircraft parts. No effect to the aircraft.
Moderate – Substantial build up of ice. Airspeed loss can affect safety of aircraft.
Severe – Accretion is sufficiently great to endanger the aircraft’s performance. Change heading or altitude is advisable.
Thunderstorm Requirements
A well developed Cb cloud. This implies a trigger action.
An unstable atmosphere.
Large moisture content.
A mechanism to produce a potential electrical difference between the cloud and its surroundings. (More for the development of lightning).
The trigger can be caused by a front, orographic lifting, convection or low-level convergence.
The adequate supply of moisture provides the ‘fuel’ for the Cb development through the release of latent heat as the cloud forms.
The release of latent heat destabilises the atmosphere and accelerates the updraughts.
This causes more cloud to form, which releases more latent heat, which accelerates the updraughts.
This feedback mechanism feeds what is effectively a huge heat engine. Moisture content at ground level also determines the height of the cloud base.
Stage One – Growing Stage
Strong updraughts cause large amounts of moisture to be carried aloft. Some of this moisture turns to ice and latent heat is released.
The updraughts continue due to the latent heat release. Large Cb clouds form.
Stage Two – Mature Stage
The water drops coalesce or collide until they are too heavy to be supported by the updraughts and start to fall.
Some of the water is re-absorbed into the cloud and latent heat is also absorbed, resulting in strong cool downdraughts.
Precipitation from the base of the cloud indicates the mature stage.
This precipitation can be made up of hail and heavy rain.
Stage Three – Decaying Stage
The downdraughts weaken the updraughts and limit the supply of moisture to upper levels of the cloud.
The cloud collapses and dissipates to Cu or St.
Turbulence/Draughts

The most serious hazard associated with thunderstorms. These vertical winds can reach speeds in excess of 5000ft per minute in New Zealand, thus generating a very violent overturning motion, enough at times to tear the wings off an aircraft.
Both updraughts and downdraughts are present. Updraughts occur mainly during growing and mature stage, while downdraughts occur during the mature and decaying stage.
Turbulence will be found in between the up/downdraughts.
Gusts
A Gust Front or First Gust is the boundary between the cold outflow air resulting from the microburst and the warm inflow air feeding a Cb.
The warmer air, being less dense, rises over the cold air, frequently creating what is known as a roll cloud on the leading edge of an advancing Cb cell.
In New Zealand, this gust front may precede the Cb cell by up to 5km and the roll cloud may not be visible if there is insufficient moisture in the air.

It is not uncommon for the surface wind to change direction by 180° instantly with the passage of the gust front, and for the wind to increase from 10 knots or so ahead of it to gusts of 40 to 50 knots behind the gust front – a wind shear of perhaps 50 or 60 knots.
Research in the United States has shown that an unexpected windshear of just 35 knots is enough for almost all pilots to lose control of their aircraft.
Cb And Windshear
Windshear is very common around Cbs. Occurs when you have different speeds or direction between differing levels.
Icing
Due to the large amounts of super condensed water droplets (SCWD), hail and ice crystals, icing is a major problem. Worst conditions will be found above the freezing level within 6-8000 feet.
Lightning
If an aircraft is struck by lightning this can burn or punch holes in the skin of the aircraft.
Other effects, are loss of aerials and magnetic compasses and electronic equipment suffering major damage.
Hail
Stones that are larger than 12mm can damage aircraft especially those at high speed.
Noise
Hail stones striking the aircraft will create large amounts of noise affecting pilot's concentration and ability to fly their aircraft.
To lessen the effects of the thunderstorms there are several steps that should be taken.
Height – the best height to fly is above the tops of the Cb clouds.
But this depends on aircraft performance to whether you can fly that high.
De-Icing Equipment – You should have your de-icing equipment turned on before entering cloud associated with Cbs.
Airspeed – should be reduced below Va if turbulence of moderate to severe strength is encountered.
Best to avoid the thunderstorm completely.
Are rotating funnels of air sucked up from below the base of Cb clouds.
This rotating air is drawn up into the cloud through convergence.
Very few Cbs develop to the stage where updraughts are strong enough to produce tornadoes.
The average life span is only a few minutes long, occasionally they last for more than one hour.
The main hazard is going to be severe turbulence especially for low flying aircraft.
There are favoured areas for their development, namely: the West Coast of the South Island, around Taranaki and on the escarpment immediately to the NW of Albany, north of Auckland.
Tornadoes are measured on the Fujita Scale which ranges from F0 to F5. F0 tornadoes cause minimal damage, while F5 tornadoes cause massive damage.
Tornadoes in New Zealand are usually F0, F1 and rarely, F2 (capable of moderate damage within a band about 100m wide and up to 1km in length.
Tornadoes which form over water are called ‘waterspouts’ and those which do not touch the ground are called funnel clouds.
An example of a Föhn Wind is the Canterbury Nor ’wester.
A Föhn wind may be experienced if a mountain range forms a barrier to a wind flow.
The prerequisites for a Föhn wind to form are:
A substantial mountain range.
A wind blowing more or less at right angles to the mountains.
A high moisture content of the approaching air.
As the air is forced upward, it initially cools at the Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR) until the Rising Condensation Level (RCL) when it cools at Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR).
Cloud will form in various forms dependent on the stability of the air.
Precipitation is likely to fall, and the water content will be reduced.
Because the water content has been reduced, the dew point has also reduced.
As the air starts descending it warms at the SALR and the temperature soon meets the new dew point where the cloud base will be.
The air now warms at the DALR for a far greater distance which results in a higher temperature than the windward side, it will be drier and gusty.
Cloud bases will be extremely low (perhaps 100 to 500ft AMSL), often with heavy precipitation and very poor visibility.
Frequent embedded thunderstorms are also a distinct possibility.
Definitely NOT VFR flight conditions.
About and immediately to the West of the ridge line, conditions will be like those explained in windward side.
Above, with the addition of extremely strong winds, especially through the passes and valleys leading up to them.
Immediately to the East of the ridge line, there will be a rapid clearance of most of the cloud below the mountain tops.

This is because the air immediately in the lee of the mountain range is ‘dumping’ and therefore warming up causing the cloud to evaporate. Often, a layer of higher cloud with bases around 15 – 20,000ft will exist.
Often the precipitation doesn’t stop, as large rain droplets can be blown well downstream and appear to fall from relatively clear skies.
Visibility in this rain is usually not bad, however, as the droplets are widely spaced. So, weather wise, flight conditions in the East could best be described as OK for VFR flight.

However, the big problem will be the large areas of moderate to severe turbulence at heights between ground level and about 1.5 times the height of the range. At times, in strong flows, this turbulence may border on extreme, especially in rotor zones.
If the ELR is less than 1.5°C, rising saturated air will be stable and the cloud formed will be stratiform.
If the ELR is greater than 1.5°C/1000ft, the rising saturated air will be unstable, and the cloud will be cumulus.

lessons.title: Small Scale Interference to Wind Flow

content.content: By small scale, we are referring to buildings, shelter belts and similar obstructions.
A pressurised area forms on the windward side of the obstruction which can extend to 5 times the height of the obstruction.
As the airflow bends over the obstruction, a venturi effect will accelerate the flow above and slightly to the lee of the obstruction, this is strongest up to 3 times the height of the obstruction.
The flow can be disturbed down wind as far as 50 times the height of the obstruction and substantial turbulence can be experienced up to 20 times the height of the obstruction.

Although similar in principle to small scale interference, mountain wave also known as Standing Wave or Lee Wave, can produce spectacular cloud formations and severe turbulence and involve hundreds of miles of sky.
The prerequisites for the formation of mountain waves are:
A mountain range of substantial dimension.
A wind more or less at right angles to the range.
The low-level wind must be at least 15 knots and increase in strength with height.
A generally unstable atmosphere at low levels with a stable layer at altitude, normally slightly higher than the mountain crests. The air above this layer should be less stable or slightly unstable.
The cloud forms, then evaporates on the way down, then reforms.
The vertical currents have been known to reach 3500ft/min but are more usually 1000 – 1500ft/min.
The axis of oscillation may lean into wind, putting the crest over lower-level troughs.
The wavelength can be 3 – 25 km or more.
The amplitude can be thousands of feet.
Wavelength largely depends upon the speed of the wind.
The faster the wind, the larger the wavelength.
The length of the lee side also has a large influence on wavelength.
Amplitude is governed by the shape and size of the mountains.
The higher the mountain, the greater the amplitude potential.
When a series of ridges obstructs the flow of air, the amplitude will be greatly increased if the distance between ridges equals the wavelength.
If the distance is more or less, they will dampen the amplitude.
These can be found in the lee of the mountain at mountain crest height if the amplitude is large.
When cloud is present, it will show as ragged and rapidly rotating streaks with the tumbling axis parallel to the mountain range.
Turbulence and downdraughts can be and are severe.
In mountain wave conditions, approach the range with as much height as possible to avoid the rotor zone.
The low-level wind is effectively caught in the undertow of the land.
Rotors are extremely turbulent and have destroyed aircraft in flight in New Zealand.
Often the rotor zone will form in a reduced moisture environment. When this happens, the rotor still exists, but there will be no cloud to signal its existence.
For this reason, flight in the zones where rotors are likely to exist should be avoided at all cost. The favoured areas for rotors to form are:
Under the crests of each wave system (indicated by the presence of high-level lenticular cloud.
Immediately in the lee of the ridge-line at about ridge-top height.
At higher levels, in the troughs of the wave system between lenticular cloud lines.
At very low-levels when the Northwest wind is touching down at the surface.
Any cloud that forms on the windward side will be cumulus, considering the low-level requirement for instability.
Some of the cloud may run down the valleys on the lee side, this will be the only low-level cloud on the lee side.
The clouds that form at altitude on the lee side are known as lenticularis.
As the air rises, it experiences adiabatic cooling, then as it descends, adiabatic warming, it is important to note that the cloud is not just drifting downwind.
The wave system can extend to 80,000ft over the Southern Alps while gliders have soared to 36,000ft in the Wairarapa of hills about 5000ft high.
This requires a change in one of the prerequisites, such as a substantial change in wind direction or stability.
Approaching weather systems such as fronts often provide this change.
When a strong wind blows onto a mountain range and the speed of this wind decreases in strength from crest level upward, it is likely that rotor streaming will develop.
Rotor streaming is caused by the enhanced venturi effect of the slower air above crest height which results in very high wind speeds at low levels on the lee side.
Flight above crest height will be considerably more comfortable and safer.
Cloud Base,
Turbulence,
Adverse & Favourable wind,
Visibility,
Track Selection,
Anticipated timing of any expected weather change.
As a rule, the cloud base will be much lower on the windward side of the ranges – often unflyable.
On the lee side of the divide, cloud bases will be high – often well above the highest ridges.
Some lower-level cloud may exist in the form of rotor clouds.
These should be avoided at all costs. Cloudscapes in mountainous terrain can change very rapidly.
A slight increase in moisture advected into an area of rising air can result in the sudden formation of cloud where none existed previously.
Always keep checking behind you to ensure your escape route remains open.
Cloud that is forming rapidly above or about far of ridges is a good indication that dew point temperatures are rising.
Rising dew points generally mean more cloud development and lowering bases, and such cloud development can occur rapidly in mountainous terrain.
To windward, light to moderate turbulence is common.
Severe turbulence, though possible, is rare except in thunderstorms.
In the lee of the ranges, severe turbulence is relatively common, especially in rotor zones, but it’s also possible anywhere within the friction layer.
In some valleys, the flow will align itself with the valley – either up it or down it. Flying in these valleys is generally not a problem.
However, the wind may be across the valley, and this frequently sets up a rotation in the vertical which could be clockwise or counter-clockwise depending on wind and terrain considerations.
It would be advisable to establish which side of the valley is up drafting, and which side is down-drafting.
Avoid the down-drafting side if possible – the combination of rising ground and descending air can be disastrous.

Make use of up-drafting air – it’s much safer to fly in the updraughts in mountainous environments – but keep an eye out for other traffic – pilots flying the other way may have the same idea of flying on the up-drafting side of the valley.
Generally, visibility will be poor on the windward side of the range in rain, drizzle or snow.
On the lee side visibility is usually very good; however, curtains of rain or virga may exist some distance downstream from the main divide.
There are, of course, exceptions when pockets of poor visibility may still exist on the lee side, particularly if a front is passing overhead.
In very strong winds, visibility at low-levels in east coast valleys may be reduced due to blowing dust and sand, especially after extended dry spells in the braided river systems.
Another problem associated with visibility is one related to visual illusions and loss of horizons.
Superimpose the horizon through terrain, this line on the mountains in front of you. This will help you maintain both attitude and altitude.
Use the coast if need be.
Plan a route through the passes etc. to your destination, but always be prepared to change your plans if the passes are closed due weather. And of course, be wary of a pass closing behind you.
With little or no indication as to which way the wind is rotating in some valleys, choosing the correct side of the valley to fly in may be problematical.

When flying up or down a valley with a high traffic density (around Mt Cook for example), you should always fly on the right-hand side so that opposing traffic will always be on the opposite side of the valley. Careful of downdraft though.
NEVER enter a valley which is too narrow to do a 180° turn in.
When crossing a ridge, do so at a 45° angle. If sink is encountered, the turn back towards safety will be at a shallower angle of bank with less wing loading and less distance to cover.
Always be wary of sink approaching the ridge-line, or during any turn-back. In stronger winds, expect stronger sink, so approach ridge-lines at a greater height.

The wind blowing through passes or saddles is often stronger than the wind blowing over the higher ridge-lines. If you get lost flying in the ranges, follow the biggest valley you can find downstream.
Not only will the valley tend to broaden downstream, but it will eventually lead to bigger rivers, roads, and towns where you can re-orientate yourself.
Synoptic Observation
Collection and analysis of weather observations over a large area. Made at standard times during the day.
Polar Front Theory
Developed in the 1920s by Norwegian meteorologists. The theory said there was a zone called the Polar Front which separated the very cold polar air from the warm air of the tropics.
Along the Polar Front, you have advancing cold air and warm air, (fronts).
Air Mass

An airmass is defined as a large body of air whose physical characteristics, especially temperature and humidity, are approximately the same, level for level, over large horizontal distances (hundreds or thousands of kilometres).
They generally form under stationary anticyclonic conditions where winds remain light for a period of at least five days.
Air Mass Categories
Arctic Continental (Ac)
Polar Continental (Pc)
Polar Maritime (Pm)
Tropical Continental (Tc)
5. Tropical Maritime (Tm)
Arctic Continental
This airmass is not found in New Zealand. But its characteristics are that it is extremely dry and very cold.
Due to temperature, there is very little moisture present therefore little or no cloud and precipitation.
Polar Continental
Also not found in New Zealand as any Polar air must track over oceanic areas thereby making it a Polar Maritime airmass.
Polar Maritime
Very dry and cold initially as it travels North, warms slightly and picks up moisture.
Moderate to heavy precipitation especially in Southern areas. The East and West coasts of New Zealand can expect generally fine conditions with the odd shower.
Northern areas will be fine, as the airmass will have run out of moisture.
Tropical Continental
Not found in New Zealand. Occurs in Central Australia. Due to lack of moisture conditions are very hot, dry and unstable. Dust storms and even tornadoes can develop.
Tropical Maritime
Is found in New Zealand. Warm and moist airmass which cools from below as it travels South and becomes more stable.
Weather conditions to be expected are drizzle, low cloud and fog in the North and Eastern parts.
While in the Southern and Western areas conditions should be fine.
Cold & Warm Advection
Cold Advection
Occurs when cold air moves over a warmer region. Conditions in NZ during cold advection are heavy shower activity on the West coasts while the East remains relatively sheltered.
Warm Advection
During warm advection, low cloud/fog with drizzle occurs in Northland, Auckland, Marlborough Sounds and Nelson, with the rest of the country unaffected.
Depressions
Mid Latitude Depressions
Most common type of depression. Air moves poleward from the tropics.
Convergence of low and mid-Troposphere air will cause this air to rise. An extensive cloudband will form. Layered cloud such as As and Ns can be expected along with varying amounts of precipitation.
Polar Depressions
Due to low level convergence, there is strong upward motion of the air. With mainly cumulonimbus cloud to be found.
Usually shown on a weather map as a cold front even though temperature contrast is slight.
Fronts As Shown On Weather Maps
When shown on weather maps, a cold front is blue, warm fronts are in red, occluded fronts are purple and a stationary front is blue/red.
A cold front is a boundary between a mass of cold air advancing on warmer air.
Rapid Movement – 15 to 40Kts.
Marked temperature drop as the front goes through.
Marked wind change from the northerly quarter to the SW quarter.
Sharp pressure rise in the heavier cold air behind the front.
Convective clouds with the showers of rain, hail, snow or sleet.
Narrow band of precipitation, usually just prior to the front.
A warm front is advancing warm air which overtakes colder air. The front face is quite shallow when compared to a cold front.
Slow movement – 5 to 15kts.
Temperature rises behind the front with clearing weather.
Wind change from the ENE to NW, but not as marked as with cold front.
Extensive sheet of layer cloud for hundreds of kms ahead of the surface front.
Cloud gradually thickens and lowers over the 24 – 36hrs.
Rain falling from As and Ns for prolonged periods ahead of the surface front.
Possible low-level St and Fog in saturated air beneath frontal As, Ns, due rain.
Stationary Front
Officially, any front that slows down to less than 5 knots ground speed is redrawn as a stationary front.
This explains why stationary fronts drawn on a series of weather maps often appear to move substantially over a 24-hour period.
Stationary fronts are often weakening fronts, however on occasion; they can result in an extended (2-3 day) period of extremely poor weather if they stall overhead.
Occluded Front
Two types, cold and warm occlusions.
Cold occlusions occur when you have a cold front overtaking a warm front.
Warm occlusions occur when cold air overtakes colder air and forces the warm sector aloft.
Occluded fronts are drawn on weather maps when there is a band of precipitation, but it lacks the characteristics of a cold or a warm front.
The classical occlusion forms when a cold front catches up with a preceding warm front, lifting the frontal boundary completely of the surface.
They therefore tend to have a weak temperature gradient at low-levels.
However, precipitation continues from the elevated frontal boundary, and the precipitation still falls to the surface.
Cold air moving over a warmer surface (warmer oceans).
Air heated from below.
Results in UNSTABLE conditions.
Convection.
Cumuliform Cloud (Cb, TCu, Cu).
Showery conditions, sometimes heavy.
Warm air moving over a colder surface (colder oceans).
Air cooled from below.
Results in stable conditions.
Stratiform cloud (St, Sc, Ns, As).
Possible widespread drizzle or rain.
Windshear is defined as:
A sudden change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance, either horizontally or vertically.
Thus, windshear creates tumbling motions within the atmosphere which are experienced by aircraft as turbulence.
Windshear occurs when you have varying wind direction and or speed within short horizontal or vertical distance.
Turbulence will be greatest when you have low level stability with higher level instability and at dawn when the friction layer is at its most dense.
Windshear, as was stated earlier, is a change in wind speed, direction or both in the horizontal or the vertical.
This windshear can be encountered when taking off or landing, which creates many problems e.g.
Loss of airspeed.
Reduction in lift.
Increase in rate of descent.
Likelihood of turbulence.

The first involves taking-off with a moderate to strong crosswind component (relative to the aircraft type), and while this may not strictly involve windshear, it is non-the-less something you need to be ready for as a pilot, otherwise, a runway excursion or a flight upset could result.

A specific example sometimes (though rarely) exists at Wellington Airport. Wellington is very much prone to terrain channelling. When the broad-scale flow over central New Zealand is Westerly, the surface wind at Wellington Airport will be from the North to NNW.

The dramatic change in wind direction from the top of the friction layer down to the surface is due to terrain channelling and friction. The windshear will be greatest when the air mass is stable. But if conditions are unstable (e.g. with lots of convection), the shear is less, and the occasional strong Westerly gust may push down to the surface, creating a significant, but short-lived cross-wind on the Wellington Airport runway.

If a strong crosswind is present or encountered whilst taking off, control corrections will be required to combat the natural tendency for the aircraft to weathercock into the wind, or to prevent a wing-drop, or worse.
The second happens if a major wind-shift is encountered during the take-off roll or soon after it.

If, whilst taking off into a headwind, you suddenly encounter a strong tailwind, the take-off roll distance will increase markedly as your aircraft struggles to accelerate to the required airspeed for take-off.
If encountered shortly after take-off, you may encounter significant sink, and even if the aircraft doesn’t sink, the rate of climb and the angle of climb will both be reduced.
This type of shear also comes with a fair amount of turbulence, so you will also have to deal with this whilst fighting to get the aircraft safely away from the ground.

There is one bright light on the horizon in this situation, however. It is very unlikely that you will ever encounter such a major wind shift on take-off, without there being some significant visual indications to warn you of the impending wind change.
Most wind direction and speed changes of this nature at or near ground level, are the result of a gust front associated with an approaching cumulonimbus cloud.
If you suspect an approaching thunderstorm is close by, delay the take-off. In addition, be wary of high based Cb clouds, especially if they have virga falling from their base.
Stronger wind-shears are often associated with these higher based clouds due to the cooling effect of the evaporation accelerating the downdraughts.
Trials on low-level wind-shear and has determined that a 35-knot windshear just above ground-level is enough to cause almost all pilots to lose control and crash the aircraft.

To put this into perspective, if a gust front associated with a travelling thunderstorm is approaching an airfield and the wind changes from a Northerly of 10 knots to a Southerly of 25 knots with the gust front, a 35-knot windshear has just occurred.

Gust fronts in New Zealand often have gusts up around the 50-knot mark, so even though our thunderstorms are relatively benign by world standards, they are still capable of causing significant low-level windshear.

The forecast 2000ft wind added to all domestic TAFs in New Zealand is there to help pilots anticipate the presence of low-level windshear. The greater the speed differential, and/or the greater the difference in the angle of the wind between the surface and 2000ft, the greater the chances of encountering low-level windshear.
There are many examples in the CAA files of aircraft in New Zealand encountering low-level windshear which has resulted in a heavy landing, or the aircraft landing short of the runway.

Above shows the flight profile of an aircraft on the approach to landing. Above, the aircraft experiences ‘sink’ as it descends into the calm layer beneath the inversion. In this instance however, the pilot has time to adjust to the windshear experienced.

In the second diagram, the sink occurs at a lower height. If the pilot applies too much power to overcome the sink, the aircraft may end up above the ideal approach path, resulting in a touchdown further into the runway.
In the above diagram, the shear-zone is encountered at very low-levels. If the pilot is slow to react to the sink, the aircraft may touchdown short of the runway.
Turbulence
Small scale, short term, random and frequent changes to velocity of air.
Thermal Turbulence
Surface heating will create vertical currents including eddies which produce turbulence.
The type of surface largely affects the degree of thermal turbulence. Is only a concern when flying very low level.
Mature Cbs contain very strong updraughts and downdrafts next to each other.
These vertical winds can reach speeds more than 5000ft per minute in New Zealand, thus generating a very violent overturning motion, sufficient at times to tear the wings of an aircraft.
Since no VFR private pilot should be caught flying inside a Cb cloud, the internal turbulence should not affect them.
Another source of turbulence associated with Cbs is caused by Microbursts – columns of rapidly descending air beneath the Cb cloud base.
Despite common misconceptions, microbursts can and do develop in New Zealand and extreme care should be exercised when considering taking of or landing with a Cb just of the end of the runway.
Almost all New Zealand’s microbursts will be ‘wet’ microbursts i.e. accompanied by rain, and therefore clearly visible. If encountered, microbursts can force an aircraft down to the ground.
Another source of convective turbulence is a by-product of the microburst. When a microburst hits the ground, it spreads out horizontally, creating a phenomenon known as a First Gust or Gust Front.

A First Gust or Gust Front is the boundary between the cold outflow air resulting from the microburst and the warm inflow air feeding a Cb. The warmer air, being less dense, rises over the cold air, frequently creating what is known as a roll cloud on the leading edge of an advancing Cb cell.
In New Zealand, this gust front may precede the Cb cell by up to 5km and the roll cloud may not be visible if there is insufficient moisture in the air.

It is not uncommon for the surface wind to change direction by 180° instantly with the passage of the gust front, and for the wind to change from 10 knots or so ahead of it to gusts of 40 to 50 knots behind the gust front – a windshear of perhaps 50 or 60 knots.
Attempting to cut in front of an approaching Cb and gust front to land into a 10-knot head wind is fraught with danger.
If the gust front catches you before touchdown, the best you can hope for is a very hard landing. It just gets worse after that.
Mechanical Turbulence
Caused by interference of surface features on the horizontal flow of air. Two types of mechanical turbulence, small and large scale.
Small Scale
Objects that are small in size which, causing turbulence found in the friction layer.
Strength depends on wind speed and stability of air. Wind speed less than 15kts produces light turbulence.
Above 15kts produces moderate turbulence.
To minimise the affect of the small-scale turbulence, fly above it, as it does not extend to a great height.
Large Scale
Applies to mountain ranges or isolated large mountains.
Degree of turbulence will depend on the stability of the air.
In stable conditions, moderate to severe turbulence can be expected at low levels in the lee of the mountains.
In unstable conditions, turbulence will occur at higher altitudes as evidenced in wave action and rotor turbulence.
As most mountains have rugged terrain, the friction or boundary layer will be deep and turbulent immediately above and in the lee of the ranges.
The turbulent zone generated beneath these waves may extent hundreds of kilometres out to sea.
Strong updraughts and, more importantly, strong downdraughts are likely to exist.
Vertical winds will often exceed the performance of your aircraft.
Low groundspeed is another hazard, although it can be advantageous too. A low groundspeed means you will be in the danger zone for longer.
Low ground speed will give you a little more time to make decisions about escaping or turning away from the ridge line.
A local low-level obstruction to the strong surface flow will create tumbling and turbulence downstream from the object.
Immediately downwind the air will be dumping toward the ground, creating a localised downdraught.
Helicopter pilots operating into pads immediately downwind of a building or a row of trees should be very cautious in strong wind scenarios.
Every aircraft in flight generates wake turbulence.
The pressure difference between the air flowing over the upper and lower surface of a wing creates wake vortices
Twisting spiral torrents of air that can trail a large distance behind the aircraft.
Strength depends on
Mass of aircraft
Aircraft configuration
Indicated airspeed.
Time delays are used between every aircraft that lands and takes off, to minimise the effect of wake turbulence.
Vortices typically persist for between one and three minutes, with their survival likely to be longest in stable air conditions with low wind speeds.
Such conditions can extend their survival at higher cruise altitudes beyond that at low level because of the lower air density there.
There are a number of different options open to a pilot in terms of avoiding wake turbulence.
An approach above and a touchdown beyond that of the generating aircraft will keep a light aircraft out of the unsafe zone.
Likewise, an early rotation and steeper climb rate than the generating aircraft will avoid the problem.
Where these options are not available, the next best option is to wait.
Light
Involves occasional movement of the aircraft around its three axes so that mild rolling, pitching and yawing may occur.
Flight control is not a problem.
Moderate
Persistent and abrupt movement around the axes. Rolling, pitching and yawing is more severe.
Flight control can generally be maintained.
Severe
Abrupt and large movement of the aircraft about the three axes. Flight control is frequently but briefly lost.
Methods To Avoid Turbulence
Altitude – by flying at higher altitudes the effect of turbulence can be reduced or eliminated.
Suitable Route – when selecting a route, fly on the windward side, if possible, where turbulence will be less.
Slow Down – effects of turbulence are greatly reduced at lower airspeeds.
If possible, fly above the top of turbulence cloud where conditions will be smoother.
New Zealand's climate is affected by three things.
Latitude
Oceanic surroundings and
Topography.
Latitude
New Zealand lies between 34 degrees South and 47 degrees South.
This means Northland is classed as a sub-tropical region, while the rest of the country is temperate.
Northland is the warmest region in the country with small fluctuations in temperature. The rest of the country has large fluctuations in temperature.
Oceanic Surroundings
With New Zealand surrounded by ocean means we have a moist climate.
Oceanic surroundings also affect the temperature variation between Summer and Winter. On the West Coast, variation is between 7-8 degrees but on the East it’s between 12-13 degrees.
Topography
With New Zealand's main mountain ranges lying SSW to NNE this creates an obstruction to the prevailing westerly winds.
This means on the West Coast generally there will be low ceilings, and reduced visibility with associated precipitation.
On the East, turbulence will be more prevalent, but there will be less precipitation and better visibility.
Another effect of New Zealand's landscape are the distinct gaps in the orographic obstruction to the westerlies for example Cook Strait and Foveaux Strait.
These gaps create a funnelling effect on the wind. This turns strong winds into gale force winds.
Northwesterly
During a North Westerly wind, gale force winds can be found between the straits.
On the West Coast, turbulence will be nil, with moderate precipitation and fair visibility outside the rain.
On the East Coast, drier conditions, with turbulence to low levels and good visibility.
Southwesterly
With a South Westerly airflow, cumulus cloud will be found on both coasts.
Showers will occur, visibility will be good outside of showers with smooth flying conditions on the West Coast.
In the East mainly fine, with turbulent conditions and good visibility.
Southeasterly
Not a common occurrence.
When it does occur, the West Coast has fine conditions with turbulence, while the East has showers , good visibility outside showers and smooth flying.
If the Southeast flow is part of a depression, it can make VFR flying not possible, due to low cloud and possibility of snow.
Northeasterly
With a Northeast airflow, the East Coast will have showers with low cloud especially in Canterbury and Otago.
Outside of the precipitation and cloud visibility will be good with smooth conditions.
On the West Coast, fine conditions with some turbulence can be expected.
Trend(Landing Forecast) appended to a METAR or a SPECI.
An indication of expected changes to those reported in a METAR or SPECI. Two-hour Validity and supersedes the applicable TAF.
NOSIG – no significant CHANGE from the reported weather is expected (ref NZOH).
BECMG (becoming) or TEMPO (temporary) used when a change forecast.
BECMG used for a gradual change.
TEMPO used to describe frequent or infrequent changes which last no more than ONE HOUR per instance. Prevailing conditions to remain those originally forecast.
For example,
SPECI NZWP 120130Z 23014KT 8000 –SHRA FEW009 BKN030 06/05 Q1027 BECMG 10KM SCT018 TEMPO FM0200 6000 BKN012CB

A SPECI is issued immediately when certain weather conditions meet certain criteria. Wind Velocity, Gustiness, Visibility, Cloud, The onset or cessation of moderate or heavy precipitation or obstruction and air temperature.
When an improvement of any of the above lasts for 10mins a new SPECI is issued cancelling the original one.
ATIS
Are take off and landing reports transmitted continuously on VHF.
AWIB
Used at unattended aerodromes, similar to ATIS.
Basic Weather Reports (BWR)
A BWR is a verbal report on actual weather conditions in the vicinity of a particular aerodrome or a place given by ATC.
A BWR may contain only wind direction, QNH, ambient air temperature, weather conditions & cloud cover.
Is a verbal report on the actual weather conditions.
Can be given out by someone who acts as pilot in command or has acceptable meteorological qualifications.

6.3.1 AIREP and AIREP Special should be completed in accordance with the AIREP Format in Table ENR 1.1-2 (AIP Vol 1, Page ENR 1.1-35), except that AIREP are not required to include section 3 (MET) data if using voice communications.
6.3.2 As set out in Table ENR 1.1-2, the minimum information required in an AIREP Special is:
aircraft position;
time of report;
flight level or altitude; and
the nature of the meteorological phenomena being experienced or observed.

6.3.3 In New Zealand domestic aviation an abbreviated AIREP Special report, as set out in 6.3.2, is known as a Pilot Report or PIREP. Such reports are accorded equal priority and significance to AIREP Special.
The blue returns inside the red polygons: These are areas of continuous moderate to heavy rain.
The yellow echoes within the light blue polygon: This is an area of continuous light rain and/or drizzle.
The blue echoes within the green ellipse: These are areas of intermittent moderate to heavy rain.
The yellow echoes within the green ellipse: These are areas of intermittent light rain and/or drizzle.

The yellowy/grey echoes within the purple polygon: This type of precipitation signature frequently indicates the presence of virga (precipitation evaporating before it hits the ground). Sometimes, light snow can also look like this.
Cloud types can be seen from the precipitation signatures displayed in radar imagery.
All the precipitation signatures are of rain or drizzle, either in continuous or intermittent form. Rain and drizzle only fall from stratiform cloud/Stable conditions.

Below, a rain-band is pushing down onto New Zealand from a sub-tropical low, which means this airmass originated in the sub-tropics. This airmass is moving south over colder oceans meaning this precipitation is falling from layered stable cloud.
Cloud types are low-level stratus, along with Stratocumulus, Nimbostratus, Altostratus and Cirrostratus.
All the precipitation is falling in the form of showers, showers of rain, hail, snow or sleet.
We can see that this airmass has come from the South of New Zealand and has travelled over warmer oceans as it heads North and is very unstable.
All the cloud types are cumuliform; Cumulus, Towering Cumulus and isolated Cumulonimbus.

content.content: How to calculate the arrival of a band of showers, or the leading edge of a swarm of showers at Hamilton Airport.
a) When the line of showers first appears on the edge of the radar image, use a water-soluble pen to draw a line along the leading edge (for example, line A drawn at 2258Z).
b) An hour or two later, check the radar again, and draw a second line along the leading edge (B at 0058Z). For the purposes of this exercise, I have used a two-hour interval.

c) Now draw parallel lines ahead of this second line with a similar spacing and continue these lines until you have drawn a line past the location you are interested in. These lines, labelled C and D, represent the approximate position of the leading edge, in this case at 0258Z and 0458Z.

d) Now you can interpolate between lines C and D to get an estimation of the arrival time of these showers – in this case, the estimate for time of arrival at Hamilton will be approximately 0445Z (4.45pm NZST, or 5.45pm NZDT).
Visible images represent the amount of sunlight being reflected back into space by the clouds or by the Earth’s surface.
Cloud free land and water will typically be dark, while clouds and snow appear bright.
Thicker clouds have a higher reflectivity and appear brighter than thinner clouds.
However, it is difficult to distinguish among low- and high-level clouds in a visible satellite image.
For this distinction, infrared satellite images are useful.
Visible images cannot be used when no solar light is available.
Infrared images represent the infrared radiation emitted by the clouds or by the Earth’s surface.
They are actually measurements of temperature.
For an infrared picture, warmer objects appear darker than colder objects.
Cloud free areas will typically be dark, but also very low clouds and fog may appear dark.
Most other clouds are bright. High level clouds are brighter than lower-level clouds.
Example One
Both of these images are from 2200 UTC. The image on the left is the visible image and on the right is the infrared.
Note the area of stratus identified earlier off the Canterbury coast (red arrow) doesn’t appear in the infrared image.

If all you looked at was the infrared image, you might think there was a lot of cloud over Dunedin. However, the visible image shows this to be a thin layer of cloud. It must be cirrus because the tops are so cold in the infrared image.
This example highlights the importance of using satellite and radar images together.
Both of these images are from the same time. This is an example of a Southwest flow over New Zealand, with lots of bubbly (cumuliform) cloud West of the country and along the East coast.
The radar shows showers clipping Banks Peninsula and running up the East coast towards Southern Wairarapa.
There are also showers appearing on the Mahia Radar.

Look at the visible image on the left and note the appearance of the cloud associated with the showers heading into Southern Wairarapa. The same type of cloud extends all the way up into Northern Wairarapa and Central Hawke's Bay, as well as right up into Gisborne.
There are no showers appearing on the radar in Northern Wairarapa, Southern and Central Hawkes Bay (the area shown by the red arrow) because they are a long way from the radar, so are below the beam.
However, we can infer from the satellite image that there are showers right up the East coast of the North Island.
